title: 16 — Set Power Series
text:
A set power series is a table \(f[S]\) for every subset of an \(n\)-element universe. Think of \(f[S]\) as the weight of an object whose label set is exactly \(S\). This is useful when labels must be distributed without overlap: vertices of a graph, people in teams, or elements of a partition. Algebraically it is
\[R[x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}]/(x_0^{2},\ldots,x_{n-1}^{2}),\]
so multiplication discards terms that reuse an element. For example, \(x^{\{0,1\}}x^{\{1,2\}}=0\) because label \(1\) was used twice, while \(x^{\{0\}}x^{\{1,2\}}=x^{\{0,1,2\}}\). This one rule turns partitions into powers and connected-component extraction into logarithms.


\[ (f*g)[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T]g[S\setminus T]. \]
The formula chooses one submask \(T\) for each \(S\), so evaluating it directly for all \(S\) costs \(O(3^n)\). The fast algorithm keeps track of cardinality. Define
\[\widehat f_k[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S,\ |T|=k}f[T],\]
which is an ordinary subset zeta transform of the layer \(|T|=k\). For each mask, convolve the short sequences \(\widehat f_0[S],\ldots,\widehat f_n[S]\) and \(\widehat g_0[S],\ldots,\widehat g_n[S]\), then Möbius-invert each layer. The entry of layer \(|S|\) is \((f*g)[S]\): reaching total size \(|S|\) forces the two chosen pieces to be disjoint. The result costs \(O(n^2 2^n)\) time and \(O(n2^n)\) memory. Unlike OR convolution, the two pieces must be disjoint.



When \(g[\varnothing]=0\), every product of more than \(n\) copies of \(g\) reuses a label, so \(g^{n+1}=0\). This nilpotence makes an apparently infinite formal series finite. Substituting \(g\) into an exponential generating series \(F(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}F_kz^k/k!\) gives
\[F(g)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}F_k\frac{g^{k}}{k!}.\]
Here \(g^k\) first chooses an ordered list of \(k\) disjoint nonempty blocks; dividing by \(k!\) forgets the order. Thus \(g^k/k!\) counts unordered partitions into \(k\) decorated blocks. If every object has a unique set of connected components and weights multiply across components, then
\[\text{all objects}=\exp(\text{connected objects}),\qquad
\text{connected objects}=\log(\text{all objects}).\]
For example, if \(A[S]\) counts all allowed structures on \(S\) and \(C[S]\) counts the connected ones, first compute \(C=\log A\) and then read \(C[U]\) for the desired vertex set \(U\). The factorials must be invertible; in small characteristic use a division-free formulation or explicit partition coefficients.
Dedicated Newton/differential recurrences compute polynomial composition, exp, and related operations in \(\Theta(n^2 2^n)\), rather than repeating subset convolution for every power. Their preconditions mirror ordinary formal power series: \(\exp(g)\) needs \(g[\varnothing]=0\), and \(\log(f)\) needs \(f[\varnothing]=1\).




A value is attached to every labelled subset and a transition partitions it: subset convolution.
Count arbitrary objects from connected ones: set-series exponential.
Recover connected objects from arbitrary ones: set-series logarithm.
Need all numbers of components: compose an EGF with a set series.
Need \(\sum_S w[S][x^{S}]g^{k}\) for every \(k\): power projection, the transpose of composition.

The modelling question comes before the transform: ask whether a label may be used by both subobjects. If yes, this is not subset convolution; it may be OR convolution or an ordinary product instead.




\(x^{S}\) denotes a square-free monomial, not an ordinary integer exponent.
OR convolution permits overlap; subset convolution does not.
Rank layers above popcount(mask) are garbage and must be cleared.
\(\exp\) needs zero constant term in its argument; \(\log\) needs constant term one.
Constants are large: test up to \(n=5\) against explicit enumeration of set partitions.

Hints

First count all bipartite spanning subgraphs on each vertex set. Then remove disconnected assemblies with a logarithm or equivalent distinguished-component recurrence.

title: 09 — Transforms on Subsets and Divisors
text:
This chapter is about changing coordinates. A convolution that appears quadratic often becomes pointwise multiplication after the correct transform. The central habit is to identify the relation among indices: subset inclusion, divisibility, or the Boolean group under XOR. The loops are short; the hard part is proving which operation the statement is actually combining.
Unless a section says otherwise, array values live in a commutative ring. The zeta/Möbius stages themselves use only addition and subtraction; a convolution also needs the pointwise products in the transformed coordinates to make sense.


For a function \(f[S]\) on subsets of an \(n\)-element universe, the subset zeta transform changes coordinates from “exactly set \(T\)” to “some subset of \(S\)”:
\[F[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T].\]
For example, if \(f[T]\) counts objects whose feature set is exactly \(T\), then \(F[S]\) counts objects using only features in \(S\). Process one bit at a time, adding the state without the current bit into the state with it; invert by subtracting in the same schedule. After processing bits \(0,\ldots,i\), the current value has summed over all ways of deleting those processed bits. This induction invariant explains the transform—not merely its loop pattern.
Both take \(O(n2^{n})\) time and \(O(1)\) extra memory. The inverse works because the Möbius function of the Boolean lattice is \(\mu(T,S)=(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}\). The bits may be processed in any order because their stages commute. Keep one bit as the outer stage, however, and invert each butterfly \((a,b)\mapsto(a,a+b)\) with \((a,b)\mapsto(a,b-a)\); changing which member of the pair receives the update changes the transform.
The superset variants switch the condition and, for masks s without bit b, update f[s] += f[s | (1<<b)]. Recognition signals include “sum over all submasks/supermasks”, compatibility masks, and inclusion–exclusion over missing features.


For \(h[S]=\sum_{A\cup B=S}f[A]g[B]\), subset-zeta both arrays, multiply pointwise, then subset-Möbius. At a fixed \(S\), the product is
\[\left(\sum_{A\subseteq S}f[A]\right)\left(\sum_{B\subseteq S}g[B]\right),\]
which counts all pairs whose union is contained in \(S\). Möbius inversion turns “contained in” back into “equal to,” leaving exactly \(A\cup B=S\). For \(A\cap B=S\), use superset-zeta instead. Complexity is \(O(n2^n)\).




XOR masks form the group \((\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{n}\): every mask is its own inverse. Its characters are the plus/minus functions \(\chi_k(x)=(-1)^{\langle k,x\rangle}\). They turn a shift by XOR into a multiplicative sign, which is why
\[\widehat f[k]=\sum_x f[x]\chi_k(x),\qquad
\widehat{f *_\oplus g}[k]=\widehat f[k]\widehat g[k].\]
The Walsh–Hadamard butterfly evaluates these characters recursively.
For an array of length \(N=2^n\), XOR inversion divides by \(N\). Thus the coefficient ring must make \(N\) invertible; over a field this is equivalent to characteristic not two. Under an odd prime modulus multiply by \(N^{-1}\). With integers, transform, multiply using a wide type, then divide exactly on inversion. OR/AND FWT uses triangular butterflies and has no normalization.
Worked example. With \(f[0]=1,f[1]=2\) and \(g[0]=3,g[1]=4\), the XOR convolution is \([1·3+2·4, 1·4+2·3]=[11,10]\). Their transforms are \([3,-1]\) and \([7,-1]\); pointwise product \([21,1]\), inverse butterfly gives \([11,10]\).



The disjoint-union convolution is
\[h[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T]g[S\setminus T].\]
Plain enumeration costs \(O(3^{n})\). Split each array by rank: \(f_k[S]=f[S]\) if \(|S|=k\), else zero. Zeta-transform every rank, form
\[H_k[S]=\sum_{i=0}^{k} F_i[S]G_{k-i}[S],\]
Möbius-transform each rank, and take \(h[S]=H_{|S|}[S]\). After inversion, the rank-\(k\) entry contains pairs with \(A\cup B=S\) and \(|A|+|B|=k\). Selecting \(k=|S|\) forces \(|A\cap B|=0\) because \(|A|+|B|=|A\cup B|+|A\cap B|\). This is why overlapping operands disappear. Time is \(O(n^{2}2^{n})\) and memory is \(O(n2^{n})\).
For \(S=\{0,1\}\), the four summands are
\[
f[\varnothing]g[S]+f[\{0\}]g[\{1\}]
+f[\{1\}]g[\{0\}]+f[S]g[\varnothing].
\]
The rank index is what distinguishes these disjoint splits from OR convolution, which would also admit overlapping pairs such as \((S,S)\).
Use it when the transition partitions a set into two labeled, disjoint parts and \(n\) is around 20. If one side can be enumerated sparsely, \(O(3^{n})\) may be smaller and easier.



On positive integers ordered by divisibility, the same idea replaces “subset” by “divisor”:
\[F[x]=\sum_{d\mid x}f[d],\qquad G[x]=\sum_{x\mid m}f[m].\]
For arrays up to \(N\), divisor zeta uses \(f[ip]\mathrel{+}=f[i]\) for every prime \(p\) and \(ip\le N\). Traverse \(i\) upward in the forward stage and downward while subtracting in the inverse, so chains \(i,ip,ip^2,\ldots\) accumulate and undo correctly. Multiple zeta uses the reversed update \(f[i]\mathrel{+}=f[ip]\): traverse \(i\) downward in the forward stage and upward while subtracting in the inverse. A linear-sieve list of primes makes the structural analogy with subset bits explicit.
For LCM convolution, “both inputs divide \(x\)” is the transformed condition, so divisor zeta, pointwise multiply, then invert. For GCD convolution, the natural condition is “both inputs are multiples of \(x\),” so use sums over multiples. The update directions above matter because an in-place stage must first accumulate a whole prime-power chain and later undo it in the reverse dependency order. Complexity is \(O(N\log\log N)\) with prime-stage transforms (or \(O(N\log N)\) with direct divisor loops).
Preconditions: indices start at 1; define deliberately whether zero exists. \(\gcd(0,x)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(0,x)\) make zero a special element, so most contest implementations handle it separately.




A | B, A & B, and A ^ B require three different transforms; visual similarity is not algebraic equivalence.
Möbius inversion must be performed in the same ring as the sums. Under a modulus, normalize subtraction.
\(O(n^{2} 2^{n})\) subset convolution becomes memory-bound first. Use contiguous rank-major storage.
SOS DP may need only one transformed array, not a convolution. Do not pay for an inverse you do not need.
For counting reachable XORs, a linear basis can beat FWT; FWT is appropriate when multiplicities/distributions matter for every XOR value.

title: 04 · Practice — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
Order matters. Foundation entries isolate a tool; later entries intentionally mix modelling and algebra. Hints stop before implementation details.



Statement · official editorial · English/Japanese
Train: inclusion–exclusion over equal positions; falling factorials.
Prerequisite: factorial combinations.



Hint 1 — recognition

Choose both injective sequences, then forbid equality at each aligned position.



Hint 2 — reduction

Fix the set of positions forced equal and contract each such pair.



Hint 3 — algorithm

Sum by the number of contracted positions, with alternating signs.





Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Train: expanding powers in the falling-factorial basis using Stirling numbers.
Prerequisite: Stirling second kind, binomial identities.



Hint 1

Replace \(k^{K}\) by a sum of falling factorials.



Hint 2

Use \(k^{\underline j}{N\choose k}=N^{\underline j}{N-j\choose k-j}\).



Hint 3

The remaining binomial sum is a power of two.





Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Train: poset-style IE / subtracting paths through earlier forbidden points.
Prerequisite: lattice-path binomials.



Hint 1

Sort forbidden points in a topological order.



Hint 2

Count all paths to a point, then subtract paths whose first bad point was earlier.



Hint 3

This is triangular DP with a binomial transition.





Statement · official editorial · Japanese (browser translation useful)
Train: tree counting transformed into one factorial-scaled convolution.
Prerequisite: binomial transform, NTT.



Hint 1

For each edge, count vertex subsets lying on both sides.



Hint 2

Rearrange the sum so the requested subset size is the outer index.



Hint 3

Reverse one factorial-scaled array to expose convolution.





Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Train: polynomial-valued tree DP and interpolation.
Prerequisite: counting order-preserving labelings; interpolation.



Hint 1

Let a subtree DP depend on the maximum permitted label.



Hint 2

The DP is a polynomial of bounded degree; children multiply and the parent takes a prefix sum.



Hint 3

Evaluate enough consecutive points, then interpolate at the huge argument.

title: 12 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
This chapter collects methods that turn an apparently huge integer range into a small algebraic object: a polynomial, a Euclidean recursion, or a continued fraction. They are especially valuable in ICPC because the statement rarely names the method. The recurring question is: what structure stays small even though the input range is huge?


A polynomial of degree at most \(d\) is determined by \(d+1\) distinct values: if two such polynomials agree there, their difference has more roots than its degree and must be zero. Lagrange interpolation constructs the unique polynomial explicitly:
\[P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{d} y_i\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-x_j}{x_i-x_j}.\]
The factor for index \(i\) is \(1\) at \(x_i\) and \(0\) at all other samples, so the sum assigns the requested value at each point. At arbitrary points this costs \(O(d^2)\) for one query. When \(x_i=i\), prefix/suffix products and factorials reduce one query to \(O(d)\) after \(O(d)\) preprocessing:
\[\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-j}{i-j}
=\frac{\prod_{j<i}(x-j)\prod_{j>i}(x-j)}{i!(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)!}.\]
Preconditions are not cosmetic: sample points must be distinct and their differences invertible. In \(\mathbb F_p\), the points \(0,\ldots,d\) therefore require \(d<p\). For many arbitrary queries use a product tree and multipoint evaluation.



Define \(\Delta P(x)=P(x+1)-P(x)\) over any coefficient ring. It is the discrete analogue of a derivative: the leading \(x^d\) terms cancel, so the degree drops by at least one. It drops by exactly one when the leading coefficient times \(d\) is nonzero; this can fail in small characteristic, as \(\Delta(x^p)=1\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). When \(1,\ldots,d\) are units, repeated differences give the Newton expansion
\[P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d} \Delta^k P(0){x\choose k}.\]
For example, \(\Delta(x^2)=2x+1\) and \(\Delta^2(x^2)=2\). This Newton basis is ideal when values are consecutive or arguments shift repeatedly. Over a characteristic-zero field (more generally a \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra), or when \(1,\ldots,d+1\) are units in the coefficient ring, it also proves that if \(P\) has degree \(d\), then
\[S(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}P(i)\]
has degree \(d+1\), because \(\Delta S=P\) and its leading coefficient is the leading coefficient of \(P\) divided by \(d+1\). Therefore evaluate \(S(0),\ldots,S(d+1)\) directly and interpolate at huge \(n\). More generally, the needed condition is that all denominators in this Newton/interpolation basis are units. In small characteristic, \(S\) may not be representable by a polynomial of the expected degree, so the ordinary consecutive-point method is not licensed.
Recognition signal: fixed exponent/degree, enormous upper bound, modular answer. Do not interpolate if the degree depends on \(n\) or if sample denominators vanish modulo the chosen prime.



Define
\[F(n,m,a,b)=\sum_{0\le i<n}\left\lfloor\frac{ai+b}{m}\right\rfloor,\]
with nonnegative inputs and \(m>0\). First strip quotient parts. Writing \(a=q_am+a'\) and \(b=q_bm+b'\) separates full multiples of \(m\), whose floors are ordinary arithmetic progressions:
\[a=q_am+a',\quad b=q_bm+b'.\]
Exactly,
\[
F(n,m,a,b)=q_a\frac{n(n-1)}2+q_bn+F(n,m,a',b').
\]
Now consider the normalized remainder with \(0\le a,b<m\). The sum counts lattice points \((i,j)\) with \(0\le i<n\) and \(1\le j\le(ai+b)/m\). Let \(y=an+b\), the numerator one step beyond the final \(i\); this is the boundary used by the half-open rectangle. If \(y<m\), no point reaches the first horizontal level and the remainder is zero. Otherwise \(a>0\); put \(q=\lfloor y/m\rfloor\) and \(r=y\bmod m\). On horizontal row \(1\le j\le q\), substitute \(t=n-i\) in \(jm\le ai+b=y-at\); the number of points on that row is \(\lfloor((q-j)m+r)/a\rfloor\). Summing and reindexing \(q-j=0,\ldots,q-1\) swaps the axes and yields
\[F(n,m,a,b)=F(\lfloor y/m\rfloor,a,m,y\bmod m)\]
after the parameter update \((n,m,a,b)\leftarrow(\lfloor y/m\rfloor,a,m,y\bmod m)\). Normalize again at the start of the next iteration: the new numerator coefficient is the old modulus and may be at least the new denominator. For example, \(F(4,7,3,2)=0+0+1+1=2\), and the update gives \(F(2,3,7,0)\); stripping \(7=2\cdot3+1\) gives \(2+F(2,3,1,0)=2\). This is the Euclidean algorithm geometrically, so there are \(O(\log m)\) iterations.
Use __int128 when products can exceed 64 bits. For negative \(a\) or \(b\), first use mathematical floor division to normalize them; C++ truncating division is not floor division.
Applications include counting lattice points, sums of residues, Beatty sequences, and recursively counting points constrained by rational lines.



Euclid’s quotients form the finite simple continued fraction of a positive rational number, and the same process gives an infinite expansion for an irrational number \(\alpha\):
\[\alpha=[a_0;a_1,\ldots].\]
Convergents satisfy
\[P_i=a_iP_{i-1}+P_{i-2},\qquad Q_i=a_iQ_{i-1}+Q_{i-2},\]
starting with \((P[-2],P[-1])=(0,1)\) and \((Q[-2],Q[-1])=(1,0)\). For an irrational \(\alpha\), its convergents are best approximations of the second kind: no fraction \(p/q\) with \(0<q<Q_i\) has a smaller value of \(|q\alpha-p|\) than \(|Q_i\alpha-P_i|\). (For a rational input, the final convergent is the number itself.) The recurrence is just the record of successive Euclidean quotients, so it also supplies the Bezout-like identity below. For other bounded-denominator objectives, the optimum may be a convergent or an intermediate (semiconvergent), so derive the relevant comparison rather than citing “best approximation” without a definition. Adjacent convergents obey \(P_iQ_{i-1}-P_{i-1}Q_i=\pm1\), a built-in error check.
Use continued fractions for best rational approximations, modular inequalities, and Pell equations. Compare rationals with cross multiplication in __int128, never floating point.



For nonsquare \(D>0\), Pell’s equation is
\[x^{2}-Dy^{2}=1.\]
The continued fraction of \(\sqrt D\) is periodic. The first convergent satisfying the equation gives the fundamental solution \((x_1,y_1)\) with \(x_1,y_1>0\). Multiplication of numbers \(x+y\sqrt D\) preserves \(x^2-Dy^2\), which explains why every solution with \(x>0,y>0\) follows from
\[(x_k+y_k\sqrt D)=(x_1+y_1\sqrt D)^{k},\]
or the recurrence
\[x'=x_1x+Dy_1y,\qquad y'=x_1y+y_1x.\]
For \(x^{2}-Dy^{2}=N\), existence and seed generation are subtler; do not assume the \(N=1\) theorem transfers unchanged. Contest tasks often bound the search enough to find seeds and then advance each orbit by the fundamental unit.
Values grow exponentially. Use big integers or stop with division-based overflow checks before multiplication.



For \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), the equation \(ax+by=c\) has an integer solution iff \(g=\gcd(a,b)\) divides \(c\): the left side is always a multiple of \(g\), and Bézout constructs one whenever that necessary condition holds. Extended Euclid finds \(u,v\) with \(au+bv=g\); scale by \(c/g\). All solutions are
\[x=x_0+k\frac bg,\qquad y=y_0-k\frac ag.\]
If \(a=b=0\), all integer pairs solve the equation when \(c=0\), and none solve when \(c\ne0\); keep that degenerate case outside an extended-gcd routine.
Intersect this parameterization with sign or interval constraints using correct floor/ceiling division. A congruence \(ax\equiv c\pmod m\) is the same equation \(ax+my=c\); after dividing by \(\gcd(a,m)\), invert in the reduced modulus.
For nonlinear-looking determinant constraints such as \(ad-bc=k\), fixing two variables often reduces the rest to Bézout. For quadratic forms, factorization, modular obstructions, descent, or Pell reduction may apply.



The Stern–Brocot tree contains every positive reduced rational exactly once. Left/right runs are the continued-fraction coefficients, so whole runs can be jumped rather than traversed one edge at a time. Under a denominator or value bound, compare the two boundary fractions by __int128 cross multiplication and take the largest legal run.
Functions such as \(\min_{0\le i<n} (ai+b) \bmod m\) use the same Euclidean geometry as floor_sum: quotient away full multiples, then swap axes after the first wrap. Keep half-open interval conventions consistent.



Bernoulli numbers are defined by
\[\frac{x}{e^{x}-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}B_k\frac{x^{k}}{k!}.\]
With the convention \(i^0=1\) even at \(i=0\), they give for \(d\ge0\)
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^{d}=\frac1{d+1}\sum_{j=0}^{d}{d+1\choose j}B_j n^{d+1-j}.\]
This computes all power-sum formulas through one FPS inversion and factorial scaling. Check the \(B_1\) sign convention and require all denominators through \(d+1\) to be invertible. For one degree and one query, consecutive-point interpolation is often simpler; Bernoulli preprocessing wins for many degrees.




C++ % and / on negatives do not implement Euclidean remainder/floor division.
Lagrange denominators vanish if the interpolation degree reaches the modulus.
Inferring “it is polynomial” from samples is not a proof; establish a degree bound.
\(a*n+b\) can overflow before the floor sum shrinks it.
Pell recurrences need all seed orbits for generalized equations.
Extended-GCD coefficients may overflow even if the final normalized answer fits.

title: 08 — Generating Functions and Coefficient Extraction
text:
A generating function (GF) is a modelling language: its coefficient of \(x^n\) records the number or weight of size-\(n\) objects. An FPS is the algebra used to compute it. The critical skill is translating a construction of objects into an equation before choosing an algorithm; never start with a familiar closed form before saying what its coefficient counts.


An ordinary generating function (OGF) stores \(A(x)=\sum a_nx^{n}\). Its product splits an integer size: \([x^{n}]AB=\sum_ia_i b_{n-i}\). If an object is a left piece of size \(i\) and a right piece of size \(n-i\), the product counts all such pairs. Use it for sequences, weights, paths and otherwise unlabelled atoms.
An exponential generating function (EGF) stores \(\widehat A(x)=\sum a_nx^{n}/n!\). Its product distributes a set of labels:
\[
n![x^n]\widehat A\widehat B=\sum_i{n\choose i}a_i b_{n-i}.
\]
The binomial coefficient chooses which \(i\) of the \(n\) labels go to the first component; that is why EGFs divide by factorials. Use them when a global set of distinct labels is partitioned among components. OGFs can still describe ordered objects; the distinction is how size is distributed, not whether the English word “sequence” appears. A useful labelled-class dictionary is:



construction
EGF




disjoint choice
\(A+B\)


labelled product
\(AB\)


sequence of \(A\)
\(1/(1-A)\)


set of \(A\) components
\(\exp(A)\)


cycle of \(A\) components
\(\log(1/(1-A))\)



The last three require \(A(0)=0\), otherwise an unrestricted sequence or set can contain infinitely many size-zero components. Examples: permutations are sets of cycles, so their EGF is \(\exp(\log(1/(1-x)))=1/(1-x)\). Set partitions are sets of nonempty sets: \(\exp(e^{x}-1)\). In both examples, the expression is a literal translation of how the object is assembled.



If \(a_n=\sum_{i=1}^{d} c_i a_{n-i}\), multiply by \(x^{n}\) and sum all valid \(n\). Every shifted sequence contributes \(x^iA(x)\) except for its initial terms, which become a small correction polynomial. Thus
\[
A(x)=\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)},\qquad Q(x)=1-\sum_{i=1}^dc_ix^i,
\]
where \(P=(A_{<d}Q)\bmod x^d\) and \(A_{<d}\) contains the given initial terms. Conversely, compare coefficients in \(Q(x)A(x)=P(x)\) beyond degree \(\deg P\): a rational OGF gives a constant-coefficient linear recurrence. This equivalence lets you choose among:

DP: \(O(nd)\), good for small \(n\);
polynomial inverse: first \(n\) terms in \(O(M(n))\);
Kitamasa: one huge term in \(O(d^{2}\log n)\);
Bostan–Mori: one huge term in \(O(M(d)\log n)\).




To find \([x^{k}]P(x)/Q(x)\), multiply top and bottom by \(Q(-x)\). The denominator \(Q(x)Q(-x)\) contains only even powers: every odd term cancels with its negated partner. Let \(R(x)=P(x)Q(-x)\). An even denominator never mixes even and odd numerator coefficients, so replace \(R\) by its even-indexed coefficients if \(k\) is even and by its odd-indexed coefficients if \(k\) is odd; then replace \(x^2\) by \(x\) in both the retained numerator and the even denominator, and halve \(k\). This preserves exactly the requested coefficient while halving its index.
For the Fibonacci OGF \(x/(1-x-x^2)\) and target \(k=5\), one step gives \(R=x+x^2-x^3\) and the even denominator \(1-3x^2+x^4\). Keeping odd coefficients and replacing \(x^2\) by \(x\) reduces the query to
\[[x^2]\frac{1-x}{1-3x+x^2}=5.\]
This is the same fifth Fibonacci coefficient, with the index already halved.
Require \(Q[0]\) to be a unit and trim degrees after multiplications. If \(\deg P\ge\deg Q\), first divide \(P=SQ+R\) (which additionally requires the leading coefficient of \(Q\) to be a unit): the answer is \([x^k]S+[x^k](R/Q)\). Replacing \(P\) by \(P\bmod Q\) without retaining the polynomial part \(S\) is wrong for indices within \(S\). If polynomial division is unavailable in the ring, terms of \(P\) above degree \(k\) may still be discarded, because \(Q^{-1}\) has no negative powers; the complexity must then be stated in terms of the remaining numerator degree as well as \(d\). With \(\deg P<\deg Q=d\), complexity is \(O(M(d)\log k)\).



Recursive objects often give implicit equations. For plane rooted trees whose root has an ordered sequence of subtrees, choosing the root contributes \(x\) and choosing zero, one, two, … children contributes \(1+T+T^2+\cdots\), hence \(T=x/(1-T)\). Binary trees with allowed node-weight inventory \(W(x)\) are either empty or a root plus an ordered left and right subtree, hence \(F=1+WF^2\). Specify the empty object and whether children are ordered before solving.
Some equations can be evaluated with FPS inv/sqrt/exp; others are better used directly for coefficient extraction by Lagrange inversion.



For \(\Phi\in R[[t]]\), the equation \(T(x)=x\Phi(T(x))\) recursively determines a unique \(T\in xR[[x]]\): the coefficient of \(x^n\) on the right depends only on coefficients of \(T\) below degree \(n\). It says that every \(T\)-object is a root atom followed by a \(\Phi\)-structured collection of smaller \(T\)-objects. Instead of recursively expanding it, Lagrange inversion extracts one coefficient directly. For \(n>0\) and integer \(k>0\), it gives
\[
[x^n]T(x)^k=\frac{k}{n}[t^{n-k}]\Phi(t)^n,
\]
and more generally
\[
[x^n]H(T(x))=\frac1n[t^{n-1}]H'(t)\Phi(t)^n.
\]
These divided forms assume that \(n\) is invertible in the coefficient ring. Over characteristic \(p\le n\), the corresponding identity after multiplying through by \(n\) remains valid but may no longer determine the wanted coefficient. Use a small-characteristic method; division by \(n\) is not justified.


Coefficient extraction is a formal residue: \([x^{n}]H(T)=\operatorname{res}_x H(T)x^{-n-1}\,dx\). Substitute \(x=t/\Phi(t)\). For this change of variables, additionally assume that \(\Phi(0)\) is a unit, so \(t/\Phi(t)\) has an invertible linear coefficient. The formal change-of-variables rule supplies \(dx=(\Phi-t \Phi')/\Phi^{2}\,dt\). Hence the residue becomes
\[
\operatorname{res}_t H(t)
\left(\frac{\Phi(t)^n}{t^{n+1}}-
\frac{\Phi(t)^{n-1}\Phi'(t)}{t^n}\right)dt.
\]
The residue of the derivative of \(H(t)\Phi(t)^n/t^n\) is zero. Rearranging that zero-residue identity turns the last display into \(\frac1n[t^{n-1}]H'(t)\Phi(t)^n\). No analytic convergence is involved. The coefficient identity also has division-free forms, but this substitution proof uses both the unit assumption on \(\Phi(0)\) and division by \(n\).
Worked example. Labelled rooted trees satisfy \(T=x \exp(T)\): the root is one distinguished label and its remaining labels form an unordered set of rooted subtrees. Then \([x^{n}]T=\frac1n[t^{n-1}]e^{nt}=n^{n-1}/n!\); multiplying by \(n!\) gives Cayley’s \(n^{n-1}\) rooted labelled trees.
Recognition signal: the unknown appears recursively on both sides, but can be rearranged to \(T=x \Phi(T)\). If the target is one coefficient, do not compute the whole compositional inverse.






Constraints such as \(i=j\) can be enforced by an auxiliary variable. If \(A(u,v)=\sum_{i,j}a_{i,j}u^iv^j\), then in \(A(x/z,z)\) the term \(a_{i,j}\) carries \(x^iz^{j-i}\), so taking the constant term keeps exactly \(i=j\): \(\sum_i a_{i,i}x^{i}=\operatorname{CT}_z A(x/z,z)\). Roots-of-unity filters select indices modulo \(m\): over a field in which \(m\) is invertible and which contains a primitive \(m\)th root \(w\),
\[
\sum_{n\equiv r\pmod m}a_nx^n=
\frac1m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}w^{-rj}A(w^jx).
\]



Products over many factor types become sums after logarithmic differentiation: \((\log F)'=F'/F\). For \(F=\prod_k(1-x^{k})^{-c_k}\), \[
[x^{n-1}]F'/F=\sum_{d\mid n} d c_d.
\] Recover \(F\) with FPS exponential or a coefficient recurrence. This is central to partition and multiset enumeration.



An algebraic or exponential GF often satisfies \(A'(x)=B(x)A(x)\) or another coefficient-friendly differential equation. With sparse \(B\), the induced recurrence can beat a general FPS routine.





EGF coefficients contain inverse factorials: usually require \(n < MOD\).
Formal division requires an invertible constant denominator.
\(T=x\Phi(T)\) always determines its zero-constant-term solution recursively. The stronger condition that \(\Phi(0)\) is a unit is needed when treating \(T\) as the compositional inverse of \(t/\Phi(t)\).
Ordered sequence, unordered set and cycle constructions are different.
A closed algebraic expression may introduce a branch; select the constant term dictated by the combinatorial class.
A huge requested index plus small rational denominator signals Bostan–Mori, not expansion through that index.

title: 08 — Generating Functions and Coefficient Extraction
text:
An ordinary generating function (OGF) stores \(A(x)=\sum a_nx^{n}\). Its product splits an integer size: \([x^{n}]AB=\sum_ia_i b_{n-i}\). If an object is a left piece of size \(i\) and a right piece of size \(n-i\), the product counts all such pairs. Use it for sequences, weights, paths and otherwise unlabelled atoms.
An exponential generating function (EGF) stores \(\widehat A(x)=\sum a_nx^{n}/n!\). Its product distributes a set of labels:
\[
n![x^n]\widehat A\widehat B=\sum_i{n\choose i}a_i b_{n-i}.
\]
The binomial coefficient chooses which \(i\) of the \(n\) labels go to the first component; that is why EGFs divide by factorials. Use them when a global set of distinct labels is partitioned among components. OGFs can still describe ordered objects; the distinction is how size is distributed, not whether the English word “sequence” appears. A useful labelled-class dictionary is:



construction
EGF




disjoint choice
\(A+B\)


labelled product
\(AB\)


sequence of \(A\)
\(1/(1-A)\)


set of \(A\) components
\(\exp(A)\)


cycle of \(A\) components
\(\log(1/(1-A))\)



The last three require \(A(0)=0\), otherwise an unrestricted sequence or set can contain infinitely many size-zero components. Examples: permutations are sets of cycles, so their EGF is \(\exp(\log(1/(1-x)))=1/(1-x)\). Set partitions are sets of nonempty sets: \(\exp(e^{x}-1)\). In both examples, the expression is a literal translation of how the object is assembled.

title: 08 — Generating Functions and Coefficient Extraction
08 — Generating Functions and Coefficient Extraction
text:
To find \([x^{k}]P(x)/Q(x)\), multiply top and bottom by \(Q(-x)\). The denominator \(Q(x)Q(-x)\) contains only even powers: every odd term cancels with its negated partner. Let \(R(x)=P(x)Q(-x)\). An even denominator never mixes even and odd numerator coefficients, so replace \(R\) by its even-indexed coefficients if \(k\) is even and by its odd-indexed coefficients if \(k\) is odd; then replace \(x^2\) by \(x\) in both the retained numerator and the even denominator, and halve \(k\). This preserves exactly the requested coefficient while halving its index.
For the Fibonacci OGF \(x/(1-x-x^2)\) and target \(k=5\), one step gives \(R=x+x^2-x^3\) and the even denominator \(1-3x^2+x^4\). Keeping odd coefficients and replacing \(x^2\) by \(x\) reduces the query to
\[[x^2]\frac{1-x}{1-3x+x^2}=5.\]
This is the same fifth Fibonacci coefficient, with the index already halved.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
This chapter turns congruences into algorithms. The recurring contest signal is that values are huge but only their residue, multiplicative order, or compatibility across several moduli matters. A congruence is an equality after we deliberately forget multiples of a modulus; it is not ordinary arithmetic with a mysterious % attached. Work through the sections in order; the final four topics assume factorization from Chapter 02.
For every division below, first ask one question: is the denominator a unit in this ring? In modular arithmetic, that question is the difference between a valid derivation and a plausible-looking wrong answer.


For a positive modulus \(m\), write \(a ≡ b \pmod{m}\) when \(m \mid (a-b)\): \(a\) and \(b\) leave the same remainder after division by \(m\). Thus \(17≡5\pmod {12}\), and replacing one by the other cannot change a later sum or product modulo \(12\). Addition and multiplication descend to residue classes, but division is conditional: \(a\) has an inverse modulo \(m\) exactly when \(\gcd(a,m)=1\). Extended Euclid gives integers \(x,y\) with
\[ax+my=\gcd(a,m).\]
This identity explains division: when \(g=1\), it reads \(ax+my=1\), so \(ax≡1\) and \(x\) is the inverse of \(a\). More generally, the values of \(ax\) modulo \(m\) are exactly the multiples of \(g=\gcd(a,m)\). Therefore \(ax ≡ b \pmod{m}\) has no solution if \(g∤b\); otherwise divide by \(g\), invert \(a/g\) modulo \(m/g\), and obtain one residue class modulo \(m/g\) (hence \(g\) solutions modulo \(m\)).
Example. \(6x≡8\pmod {14}\) becomes \(3x≡4\pmod7\), so \(x≡6\pmod7\). Modulo \(14\) this means the two solutions \(6\) and \(13\). By contrast, \(6x≡5\pmod {14}\) is impossible because every left side is even modulo \(14\).
Recognition. A repeated step on a cycle, synchronized clocks, or an equation with a coefficient that may not be invertible is a linear congruence, not “ordinary modular division.”



To merge \(x≡a \pmod{m}\) and \(x≡b \pmod{n}\), start from the first statement: every such integer has the form \(x=a+mt\). Substituting it into the second gives
\[mt\equiv b-a\pmod n.\]
It is solvable iff \(\gcd(m,n) \mid b-a\); all solutions form one class modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)\). This is a consistency check, not an optional optimization. For example, \(x≡1\pmod6\) and \(x≡3\pmod8\) are compatible because \(2\mid(3-1)\); substituting gives \(6t≡2\pmod8\), then \(t≡3\pmod4\), hence \(x≡19\pmod {24}\). The pair \(x≡1\pmod6\), \(x≡2\pmod8\) is impossible: their parities already disagree. Fold constraints one at a time, normalize each merged residue, and guard the LCM against overflow.
For pairwise coprime prime powers, CRT is a ring isomorphism \(\mathbb Z/(\prod_i p_i^{e_i})\mathbb Z \cong
\prod_i \mathbb Z/(p_i^{e_i})\mathbb Z\). This is why composite-modulus equations should often be solved locally and recombined.



For prime \(p\), every nonzero residue is invertible, so the nonzero residues form a multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^\times\). This group happens to be cyclic: there is a generator \(g\) whose powers list every nonzero residue once, and its order is \(p-1\). Consequently:

Fermat: \(a^{p-1}=1\) for \(a≠0\).
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a) \mid p-1\).
A nonzero polynomial of degree \(d\) over a field has at most \(d\) roots.
\(x^{k}=a\) can be converted into a linear congruence in exponents after choosing a primitive root.

For composite moduli, nonzero does not imply invertible, polynomial root bounds may fail, and the unit group need not be cyclic. Always identify where primality is used.
The order of \(a\) is the first positive exponent \(d\) for which \(a^d=1\); it is the length of the cycle \(1,a,a^2,\ldots\). For example, \(2\) modulo \(7\) has order \(3\) because \(2,4,1\) repeat. Assuming \(\gcd(a,m)=1\), start at \(\varphi(m)\) (or the Carmichael exponent \(\lambda(m)\)) and remove a prime factor \(q\) whenever \(a^{\operatorname{ord}/q}=1\). A primitive root has order \(\varphi(m)\); for \(m\ge2\), primitive roots exist exactly for \(m\in\{2,4,p^{k},2p^{k}\}\) with odd prime \(p\) and \(k\ge1\). Some sources add \(m=1\) by a vacuous convention; it has no relevance to modular algorithms.



The \(p\)-adic valuation \(v_p(n)\) is the exponent of \(p\) in the prime factorization of a nonzero integer \(n\): for instance \(v_2(40)=3\). It is useful to set \(v_p(0)=+\infty\) when comparing valuations of sums. It turns a question about a large product into a question about addition of exponents:
\[v_p(ab)=v_p(a)+v_p(b),\qquad
v_p(n!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor n/p^j\right\rfloor.\]
For sums, \(v_p(a+b)≥\min(v_p(a),v_p(b))\), with equality if the two valuations differ: factor out the smaller power, and the remaining sum is nonzero modulo \(p\). LTE supplies sharper forms when cancellation needs to be measured. The most used one is: for an odd prime \(p\), positive integer \(n\), distinct integers \(x,y\), \(p\mid(x-y)\), and \(p\nmid xy\),
\[v_p(x^{n}-y^{n})=v_p(x-y)+v_p(n).\]
Use valuations when divisibility by a huge power or the number of trailing prime factors is asked. For binomial coefficients,
\[v_p\binom nk=\sum_{j\ge1}\left(\lfloor n/p^{j}\rfloor-\lfloor k/p^{j}\rfloor-\lfloor(n-k)/p^{j}\rfloor\right),\]
equivalently the number of carries when adding \(k\) and \(n-k\) in base \(p\) (Kummer).
For an integer polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\), Hensel lifting upgrades a root modulo \(p^{k}\) to modulo \(p^{k+1}\). We only need to decide its next base-\(p\) digit, so try \(r'=r+t p^{k}\) with \(t\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). If \(f(r)≡0\pmod {p^k}\), the first-order expansion gives
\[\frac{f(r)}{p^k}+t f'(r)\equiv0\pmod p.\]
The quotient is an integer because \(r\) was already a root modulo \(p^k\). If \(f'(r)\not\equiv0\pmod p\), this linear equation has one \(t\), hence one lift. If the derivative vanishes, it has either no solution or every \(t\) is a solution, giving zero or \(p\) lifts—never assume uniqueness.



Given \(a^{x}≡b \pmod{m}\) with \(a\) a unit, baby-step giant-step (BSGS) searches an exponent by writing the representative \(0\le x<\operatorname{ord}(a)\) as \(x=q+nj\), where \(0\le q<n\) and \(n=\lceil\sqrt{\operatorname{ord}(a)}\rceil\). Then \(a^q=b(a^{-n})^j\). Store all small “baby” powers \(a^q\) and scan the “giant” right sides; an equality gives \(x=q+nj\). Retain the smallest baby exponent for each stored value and verify every reported candidate. If the order is not known, taking \(n=\lceil\sqrt m\rceil\) is safe for a unit modulo \(m\), since the order is at most \(\varphi(m)<m\). This group version needs \(\gcd(a,m)=1\) and costs \(O(\sqrt{\operatorname{ord}(a)})\) time and memory when the order is used. It is a meet-in-the-middle search, not a logarithm in the numerical sense. If giant steps are scanned by increasing \(j\), the table retains the smallest \(q\) for each value, and candidates \(q+nj\ge\operatorname{ord}(a)\) are discarded, the first verified collision is the smallest nonnegative solution. Other scan or hash conventions should collect and minimize the normalized candidates.
The search succeeds only when \(b\) belongs to the cyclic subgroup generated by \(a\). For example, modulo \(7\) the powers of \(2\) are \(1,2,4\); therefore \(2^x\equiv3\pmod 7\) has no solution even though both sides are units.
When \(\gcd(a,m)>1\), extended BSGS repeatedly strips \(g=\gcd(a,m)\). At each stripping step, require \(g|b\), divide \(m,b\) by \(g\), and maintain the accumulated multiplier; check small exponents along the way. This is subtle enough that a known-tested template is preferable in a contest.
Pohlig–Hellman is better when the group order is smooth: solve the logarithm modulo each prime power dividing the order, then CRT the exponent. Its hard part is the largest prime factor, roughly \(O(\sqrt{q})\) group operations.



For odd prime \(p\) and \(a\ne0\), a quadratic residue is a value \(a\) for which some \(x\) satisfies \(x^2=a\). Euler’s criterion gives \(a^{(p-1)/2}\equiv1\pmod p\) exactly for residues, and \(-1\) for non-residues. Tonelli–Shanks writes \(p-1=q\cdot2^{s}\) with odd \(q\), finds a quadratic non-residue, then cancels the current error inside the \(2\)-power subgroup. Given a non-residue, it runs in \(O(\log p+s^{2})\) modular multiplications; random sampling finds one in expected constant trials.
For the excluded prime \(p=2\), the nonzero multiplicative group has one element, and both field elements \(0\) and \(1\) are their own square roots. Euler’s criterion and Tonelli–Shanks are not needed there.
For a positive integer \(k\), first separate \(a=0\) in \(x^{k}=a \pmod{p}\): its only root in a field is \(x=0\). For nonzero \(a\), write values as powers of a primitive root: \(g^{kt}=a\). A discrete logarithm converts this to \(kt≡\log_g(a) \pmod{p-1}\). It has \(\gcd(k,p-1)\) solutions if compatible. Specialized root algorithms avoid a full discrete log; use them when constraints exceed BSGS.



Euler reduction \(a^{e} \bmod m = a^{e \bmod \varphi(m)} \bmod m\) is valid without qualification only when \(\gcd(a,m)=1\): otherwise reducing a large exponent can turn a multiple of a prime into a nonmultiple. For example, \(2^4≡0\pmod4\) but \(2^{4\bmod\varphi(4)}=2^0≡1\pmod4\). For a tower, recurse through the Carmichael chain \(m, \lambda(m), \lambda(\lambda(m)), \ldots\), but a residue alone is not enough: the caller must also know whether the true exponent exceeds a requested small cap. Compute that fact with saturating arithmetic instead of inferring it from the reduced residue. For a prime-power modulus \(p^r\), first separate \(e=0\), which gives \(1\). If \(p^r\mid a\) and \(e>0\), the residue is \(0\). Otherwise write \(a=p^v u\) with \(p\nmid u\) and \(0\le v<r\). If \(v=0\), reduce the exponent modulo \(\lambda(p^r)\). If \(v>0\), then \(a^e\equiv0\pmod{p^r}\) as soon as \(e\ge\lceil r/v\rceil\); below that threshold the exponent is small enough to retain exactly. Solve this independently for every \(p^r\mid m\) and combine the residues by CRT. This local rule is the reason the extra “is the exponent large enough?” information is necessary.
For \(x^{k}=a \bmod p\), the discrete-log reduction in Section 6 is conceptual but may be too slow. Fast algorithms split \(p-1\) into its \(\gcd(k,p-1)\) part, invert the coprime exponent part, and extract roots inside the remaining smooth subgroup. Always return and verify all roots or the required canonical root; existence is equivalent to \(a^{(p-1)/g}=1\), where \(g=\gcd(k,p-1)\) for \(a\ne 0\).




Normalize negative residues; C++ % may be negative.
Never use Fermat inversion unless the modulus is prime and the denominator nonzero.
Protect multiplication and LCM with __int128; check promised bounds before casting back.
CRT consistency is a divisibility test, not pairwise coprimality.
Distinguish a primitive root of the whole multiplicative group from an \(n\)th root of unity.
In BSGS, clarify whether the smallest solution is required and handle \(x=0\), \(a=0\), and non-coprime cases.
Hensel’s derivative-zero branch and \(p=2\) require separate analysis.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
For a positive modulus \(m\), write \(a ≡ b \pmod{m}\) when \(m \mid (a-b)\): \(a\) and \(b\) leave the same remainder after division by \(m\). Thus \(17≡5\pmod {12}\), and replacing one by the other cannot change a later sum or product modulo \(12\). Addition and multiplication descend to residue classes, but division is conditional: \(a\) has an inverse modulo \(m\) exactly when \(\gcd(a,m)=1\). Extended Euclid gives integers \(x,y\) with
\[ax+my=\gcd(a,m).\]
This identity explains division: when \(g=1\), it reads \(ax+my=1\), so \(ax≡1\) and \(x\) is the inverse of \(a\). More generally, the values of \(ax\) modulo \(m\) are exactly the multiples of \(g=\gcd(a,m)\). Therefore \(ax ≡ b \pmod{m}\) has no solution if \(g∤b\); otherwise divide by \(g\), invert \(a/g\) modulo \(m/g\), and obtain one residue class modulo \(m/g\) (hence \(g\) solutions modulo \(m\)).
Example. \(6x≡8\pmod {14}\) becomes \(3x≡4\pmod7\), so \(x≡6\pmod7\). Modulo \(14\) this means the two solutions \(6\) and \(13\). By contrast, \(6x≡5\pmod {14}\) is impossible because every left side is even modulo \(14\).
Recognition. A repeated step on a cycle, synchronized clocks, or an equation with a coefficient that may not be invertible is a linear congruence, not “ordinary modular division.”

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
To merge \(x≡a \pmod{m}\) and \(x≡b \pmod{n}\), start from the first statement: every such integer has the form \(x=a+mt\). Substituting it into the second gives
\[mt\equiv b-a\pmod n.\]
It is solvable iff \(\gcd(m,n) \mid b-a\); all solutions form one class modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)\). This is a consistency check, not an optional optimization. For example, \(x≡1\pmod6\) and \(x≡3\pmod8\) are compatible because \(2\mid(3-1)\); substituting gives \(6t≡2\pmod8\), then \(t≡3\pmod4\), hence \(x≡19\pmod {24}\). The pair \(x≡1\pmod6\), \(x≡2\pmod8\) is impossible: their parities already disagree. Fold constraints one at a time, normalize each merged residue, and guard the LCM against overflow.
For pairwise coprime prime powers, CRT is a ring isomorphism \(\mathbb Z/(\prod_i p_i^{e_i})\mathbb Z \cong
\prod_i \mathbb Z/(p_i^{e_i})\mathbb Z\). This is why composite-modulus equations should often be solved locally and recombined.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
For prime \(p\), every nonzero residue is invertible, so the nonzero residues form a multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^\times\). This group happens to be cyclic: there is a generator \(g\) whose powers list every nonzero residue once, and its order is \(p-1\). Consequently:

Fermat: \(a^{p-1}=1\) for \(a≠0\).
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a) \mid p-1\).
A nonzero polynomial of degree \(d\) over a field has at most \(d\) roots.
\(x^{k}=a\) can be converted into a linear congruence in exponents after choosing a primitive root.

For composite moduli, nonzero does not imply invertible, polynomial root bounds may fail, and the unit group need not be cyclic. Always identify where primality is used.
The order of \(a\) is the first positive exponent \(d\) for which \(a^d=1\); it is the length of the cycle \(1,a,a^2,\ldots\). For example, \(2\) modulo \(7\) has order \(3\) because \(2,4,1\) repeat. Assuming \(\gcd(a,m)=1\), start at \(\varphi(m)\) (or the Carmichael exponent \(\lambda(m)\)) and remove a prime factor \(q\) whenever \(a^{\operatorname{ord}/q}=1\). A primitive root has order \(\varphi(m)\); for \(m\ge2\), primitive roots exist exactly for \(m\in\{2,4,p^{k},2p^{k}\}\) with odd prime \(p\) and \(k\ge1\). Some sources add \(m=1\) by a vacuous convention; it has no relevance to modular algorithms.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
The \(p\)-adic valuation \(v_p(n)\) is the exponent of \(p\) in the prime factorization of a nonzero integer \(n\): for instance \(v_2(40)=3\). It is useful to set \(v_p(0)=+\infty\) when comparing valuations of sums. It turns a question about a large product into a question about addition of exponents:
\[v_p(ab)=v_p(a)+v_p(b),\qquad
v_p(n!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor n/p^j\right\rfloor.\]
For sums, \(v_p(a+b)≥\min(v_p(a),v_p(b))\), with equality if the two valuations differ: factor out the smaller power, and the remaining sum is nonzero modulo \(p\). LTE supplies sharper forms when cancellation needs to be measured. The most used one is: for an odd prime \(p\), positive integer \(n\), distinct integers \(x,y\), \(p\mid(x-y)\), and \(p\nmid xy\),
\[v_p(x^{n}-y^{n})=v_p(x-y)+v_p(n).\]
Use valuations when divisibility by a huge power or the number of trailing prime factors is asked. For binomial coefficients,
\[v_p\binom nk=\sum_{j\ge1}\left(\lfloor n/p^{j}\rfloor-\lfloor k/p^{j}\rfloor-\lfloor(n-k)/p^{j}\rfloor\right),\]
equivalently the number of carries when adding \(k\) and \(n-k\) in base \(p\) (Kummer).
For an integer polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\), Hensel lifting upgrades a root modulo \(p^{k}\) to modulo \(p^{k+1}\). We only need to decide its next base-\(p\) digit, so try \(r'=r+t p^{k}\) with \(t\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). If \(f(r)≡0\pmod {p^k}\), the first-order expansion gives
\[\frac{f(r)}{p^k}+t f'(r)\equiv0\pmod p.\]
The quotient is an integer because \(r\) was already a root modulo \(p^k\). If \(f'(r)\not\equiv0\pmod p\), this linear equation has one \(t\), hence one lift. If the derivative vanishes, it has either no solution or every \(t\) is a solution, giving zero or \(p\) lifts—never assume uniqueness.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
Given \(a^{x}≡b \pmod{m}\) with \(a\) a unit, baby-step giant-step (BSGS) searches an exponent by writing the representative \(0\le x<\operatorname{ord}(a)\) as \(x=q+nj\), where \(0\le q<n\) and \(n=\lceil\sqrt{\operatorname{ord}(a)}\rceil\). Then \(a^q=b(a^{-n})^j\). Store all small “baby” powers \(a^q\) and scan the “giant” right sides; an equality gives \(x=q+nj\). Retain the smallest baby exponent for each stored value and verify every reported candidate. If the order is not known, taking \(n=\lceil\sqrt m\rceil\) is safe for a unit modulo \(m\), since the order is at most \(\varphi(m)<m\). This group version needs \(\gcd(a,m)=1\) and costs \(O(\sqrt{\operatorname{ord}(a)})\) time and memory when the order is used. It is a meet-in-the-middle search, not a logarithm in the numerical sense. If giant steps are scanned by increasing \(j\), the table retains the smallest \(q\) for each value, and candidates \(q+nj\ge\operatorname{ord}(a)\) are discarded, the first verified collision is the smallest nonnegative solution. Other scan or hash conventions should collect and minimize the normalized candidates.
The search succeeds only when \(b\) belongs to the cyclic subgroup generated by \(a\). For example, modulo \(7\) the powers of \(2\) are \(1,2,4\); therefore \(2^x\equiv3\pmod 7\) has no solution even though both sides are units.
When \(\gcd(a,m)>1\), extended BSGS repeatedly strips \(g=\gcd(a,m)\). At each stripping step, require \(g|b\), divide \(m,b\) by \(g\), and maintain the accumulated multiplier; check small exponents along the way. This is subtle enough that a known-tested template is preferable in a contest.
Pohlig–Hellman is better when the group order is smooth: solve the logarithm modulo each prime power dividing the order, then CRT the exponent. Its hard part is the largest prime factor, roughly \(O(\sqrt{q})\) group operations.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
For odd prime \(p\) and \(a\ne0\), a quadratic residue is a value \(a\) for which some \(x\) satisfies \(x^2=a\). Euler’s criterion gives \(a^{(p-1)/2}\equiv1\pmod p\) exactly for residues, and \(-1\) for non-residues. Tonelli–Shanks writes \(p-1=q\cdot2^{s}\) with odd \(q\), finds a quadratic non-residue, then cancels the current error inside the \(2\)-power subgroup. Given a non-residue, it runs in \(O(\log p+s^{2})\) modular multiplications; random sampling finds one in expected constant trials.
For the excluded prime \(p=2\), the nonzero multiplicative group has one element, and both field elements \(0\) and \(1\) are their own square roots. Euler’s criterion and Tonelli–Shanks are not needed there.
For a positive integer \(k\), first separate \(a=0\) in \(x^{k}=a \pmod{p}\): its only root in a field is \(x=0\). For nonzero \(a\), write values as powers of a primitive root: \(g^{kt}=a\). A discrete logarithm converts this to \(kt≡\log_g(a) \pmod{p-1}\). It has \(\gcd(k,p-1)\) solutions if compatible. Specialized root algorithms avoid a full discrete log; use them when constraints exceed BSGS.

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
Euler reduction \(a^{e} \bmod m = a^{e \bmod \varphi(m)} \bmod m\) is valid without qualification only when \(\gcd(a,m)=1\): otherwise reducing a large exponent can turn a multiple of a prime into a nonmultiple. For example, \(2^4≡0\pmod4\) but \(2^{4\bmod\varphi(4)}=2^0≡1\pmod4\). For a tower, recurse through the Carmichael chain \(m, \lambda(m), \lambda(\lambda(m)), \ldots\), but a residue alone is not enough: the caller must also know whether the true exponent exceeds a requested small cap. Compute that fact with saturating arithmetic instead of inferring it from the reduced residue. For a prime-power modulus \(p^r\), first separate \(e=0\), which gives \(1\). If \(p^r\mid a\) and \(e>0\), the residue is \(0\). Otherwise write \(a=p^v u\) with \(p\nmid u\) and \(0\le v<r\). If \(v=0\), reduce the exponent modulo \(\lambda(p^r)\). If \(v>0\), then \(a^e\equiv0\pmod{p^r}\) as soon as \(e\ge\lceil r/v\rceil\); below that threshold the exponent is small enough to retain exactly. Solve this independently for every \(p^r\mid m\) and combine the residues by CRT. This local rule is the reason the extra “is the exponent large enough?” information is necessary.
For \(x^{k}=a \bmod p\), the discrete-log reduction in Section 6 is conceptual but may be too slow. Fast algorithms split \(p-1\) into its \(\gcd(k,p-1)\) part, invert the coprime exponent part, and extract roots inside the remaining smooth subgroup. Always return and verify all roots or the required canonical root; existence is equivalent to \(a^{(p-1)/g}=1\), where \(g=\gcd(k,p-1)\) for \(a\ne 0\).

title: 01 — Modular Algebra and Finite Fields
text:
Normalize negative residues; C++ % may be negative.
Never use Fermat inversion unless the modulus is prime and the denominator nonzero.
Protect multiplication and LCM with __int128; check promised bounds before casting back.
CRT consistency is a divisibility test, not pairwise coprimality.
Distinguish a primitive root of the whole multiplicative group from an \(n\)th root of unity.
In BSGS, clarify whether the smallest solution is required and handle \(x=0\), \(a=0\), and non-coprime cases.
Hensel’s derivative-zero branch and \(p=2\) require separate analysis.

title: 17 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
text:
Determinants do more than solve linear systems: their expansion is a signed sum over permutations, hence over directed cycle covers. Choosing matrix entries carefully makes unwanted covers cancel, leaving spanning trees, matchings, or parity structures. Random evaluation then turns a symbolic nonzeroness question into finite-field linear algebra.
There are two levels to keep separate throughout this chapter. A polynomial identity is exact: if a determinant polynomial is nonzero, the desired graph object exists. A random field substitution is only a fast test for that fact: a nonzero evaluated value is a witness, while a zero can be unlucky.


For an even-dimensional skew-symmetric matrix \(A\) (\(A^T=-A\) and diagonal zero), the Pfaffian is the pairing analogue of a determinant: it sums signed products over perfect pairings. For the \(2\times2\) matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\-a&0\end{pmatrix}\), the Pfaffian is \(a\) and its determinant is \(a^2\). In general it satisfies
\[\operatorname{Pf}(A)^{2}=\det A.\]
The identity explains why Pfaffian algorithms can recognize certain weighted matching structures with determinant-like cost. Eliminate pairs of rows and columns together. If pivot A[i][j] is used, swap indices into the active pair, account for the Pfaffian sign, multiply the pivot, and apply the skew-symmetric Schur-complement update. This is \(O(n^3)\) over a field of characteristic not two. The hafnian removes signs and directly counts weighted perfect pairings, but its general algorithms are exponential; do not confuse a Pfaffian with a general perfect-matching counter.



For an undirected graph, put an independent indeterminate \(x_{ij}\) above the diagonal, \(-x_{ij}\) below it, and zero on nonedges. This is its Tutte matrix. The central theorem says its determinant is a nonzero polynomial if and only if the graph has a perfect matching. One direction is intuitive from the determinant expansion: a surviving cycle cover supplies alternating edges, hence a matching; a perfect matching supplies a distinct monomial.
Substitute independent uniform field values from a set \(S\) and compute one determinant. A nonzero result certifies a perfect matching. If a perfect matching exists, an \(n\)-vertex graph gives a false negative with probability at most \(n/|S|\) per trial. Likewise, the evaluated rank is at most twice the maximum matching size and equals it with high probability. The symbolic theorem is valid in characteristic two as well, but sampling only from \(\mathbb F_2\) gives a useless error bound; use a sufficiently large field or extension field.



A nonzero polynomial of total degree \(d\) evaluated independently and uniformly over a finite set \(S\) vanishes with probability at most \(d/|S|\) (the Schwartz–Zippel lemma). Record all three quantities: degree, field size, and number of trials. With \(t\) independent trials, the bound becomes \((d/|S|)^t\). Random evaluation can produce a false zero but never a false symbolic witness. Use fresh randomness, avoid tiny fields, and repeat when the error budget is not negligible.



\(det(A+xB)\) packages a family of rank/determinant questions into one polynomial; evaluate at enough field points and interpolate. The matrix determinant lemma and Sherman–Morrison give rank-one updates when the required inverse exists. The adjugate identity
\[A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I\]
remains meaningful when \(A\) is singular and is often the safer symbolic object.




Define the symbolic matrix and prove which graph property makes its target polynomial nonzero.
Bound the total degree of that polynomial and choose a field much larger than the degree times the desired error margin.
Sample every independent entry freshly, evaluate, and run ordinary field elimination.
State the one-sided conclusion precisely: a nonzero answer is certain; a zero answer is “probably absent” with the computed error bound.





Capstone — Degree Harmony, ABC412 G. Weighted matching through determinant polynomials.


Hints

Reduce the degree constraints to a minimum-weight perfect matching; encode weights as powers of a new variable and recover the lowest nonzero degree.

Alternate-method lab — No Need, ABC056 D. Polynomial fingerprints.


Hints

Card \(i\) is necessary exactly when a subset of the other cards has sum in \([K-a_i,K)\). Replace each factor by \(1+r_jx^{a_j}\), multiply modulo \(x^K\), and divide by \(1+r_ix^{a_i}\) to exclude card \(i\). Distinct subsets give distinct square-free monomials in the formal variables \(r_j\), so the relevant coefficient polynomial cannot cancel identically. Independent uniform substitutions in \(\mathbb F_P\) turn this into a Monte Carlo test; bound the error over all tested coefficients with Schwartz–Zippel and a union bound (the official analysis obtains \(O(N^2/P)\)).

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
An FPS \(A(x)=\sum_{i\ge0}a_ix^{i}\) is an infinite coefficient sequence used as algebra in \(R[[x]]\), not an analytic function. We never substitute a real \(x\). Saying two series are equal modulo \(x^n\) means only that their first \(n\) coefficients agree. Therefore every calculation requested to precision \(n\) is finite, and an approximation with \(m\) correct coefficients can be improved systematically. This viewpoint makes Newton iteration natural.
Let \(M(n)\) be polynomial multiplication time, \(O(n\log n)\) with NTT. All operations below truncate immediately to the requested precision.


\[
A'=\sum_{i\ge1}ia_ix^{i-1},\qquad
\int A=\sum_{i\ge0}\frac{a_i}{i+1}x^{i+1}.
\]
For example, if \(A=1+2x+3x^2\), then \(A'=2+6x\). Integration divides coefficient \(x^i\) by \(i+1\). To produce coefficients of degrees below \(n\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), it therefore needs \(1,\ldots,n-1\) to be nonzero, equivalently \(n\le p\). The table records the usual contracts over a field; in a more general ring, replace every “nonzero” condition used for division by “invertible.”








operation

defining identity




\(\operatorname{inv}(A)\)
\(a_0\) is a unit
\(AB=1\)


normalized \(\log(A)\)
\(a_0\) is a unit; output constant term is \(0\)
\((\log A)'=A'/A\)


\(\exp(A)\)
\(a_0=0\); required integration denominators are units
\(\log(\exp A)=A\)


\(\operatorname{pow}(A,k)\)

\(A^{k}\)


\(\sqrt{A}\)

\(B^{2}=A\)


\(\operatorname{compose}(A,B)\)
\(b_0=0\) for finite-prefix dependence
\(A(B(x))\)


\(\operatorname{revert}(A)\)
\(a_0=0,a_1\) is a unit
\(A(B(x))=x\)






Suppose \(B\) is an inverse approximation: \(AB\equiv1\pmod{x^{m}}\). The error \(E=1-AB\) has no terms below degree \(m\). Rather than solve missing coefficients individually, correct all of them in one multiplication: \[
B_{new}=B(2-AB)\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\] Indeed \(AB_{new}=AB(2-AB)=(1-E)(1+E)=1-E^2\). Thus the old error is squared; if \(E\) starts at degree \(m\), the new error starts at degree \(2m\). Precision doubles, and the total cost over lengths \(1,2,4,\ldots,n\) is \(O(M(n))\).
Precision doubling should operate on a truncated copy so that a caller’s longer series is not accidentally destroyed.



For a unit series with constant coefficient \(1\), define the logarithm to be the unique zero-constant series whose derivative is \(A'/A\):
\[
\log A=\int A'A^{-1}\,dx,
\]
in \(O(M(n))\). More generally \(A'/A\) makes sense whenever \(A[0]\) is a unit, but the integral above deliberately discards the scalar factor \(A[0]\): it is a normalized logarithm with constant term zero. Thus \(\exp(\log A)=A\) only under the clean contract \(A[0]=1\); otherwise it equals \(A/A[0]\). The divisions from integration also require \(1,\ldots,n-1\) to be units at precision \(n\).
For exponential, the desired identity is \(\log B=A\). If \(B\) is already correct through degree \(m\), then \(A-\log B\) begins at degree \(m\), so multiplying by \(1+A-\log B\) corrects only unknown coefficients: \[
B_{new}=B(1+A-\log B)\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\]
The bracket is \(1 \bmod x^{m}\), so known coefficients remain unchanged. Standard implementations are \(O(M(n))\), though careless repeated inversions may add a constant or logarithmic factor.



When the logarithm and exponential contracts above hold, \(A(0)=1\) gives \(A^{k}=\exp(k\log A)\) because logarithm turns multiplication into addition. Here \(k=0\) is the separate identity case \(A^0=1\). For nonnegative \(k\) and a nonzero general series, find the first nonzero term \(a_tx^{t}\):
\[
A^k=x^{tk}a_t^k
\exp\!\left(k\log\frac{A}{a_tx^t}\right).
\]
If \(tk \ge  n\), the truncated answer is zero. This handles huge nonnegative \(k\) without reducing \(k\) when computing the shift; only the scalar \(k\) multiplying \(\log A\) is reduced in the coefficient field. Negative powers require a unit series and are a different contract.
Over a field of odd characteristic, solve \(B^2-A=0\). For a unit series, the ordinary Newton correction \(B-(B^2-A)/(2B)\) simplifies to \[
B_{new}=\frac12(B+A/B).
\] Start with a square root of the constant coefficient. For a nonunit \(A\), first strip an even valuation \(2t\) and solve for the remaining unit series; an odd finite valuation makes a root impossible. Tonelli–Shanks supplies the initial scalar root over an odd prime field. A unit series over an odd prime field has roots exactly when its constant coefficient is a quadratic residue; then it has exactly two, differing by sign. For a positive even valuation, shifting either unit root gives two canonical roots when the unused high coefficients are set to zero. Coefficients of \(B\) in degrees at least \(n-t\) are invisible in \(B^2\bmod x^n\) and may be arbitrary. Thus a nonunit truncated series can have more than two roots. The zero series modulo \(x^n\) is another non-unique case; choose the all-zero root unless the problem states a different normalization. Problems must specify a canonical root or accept any valid one.



Naive composition computes powers \(1,B,B^{2},\ldots\) in \(O(nM(n))\). Brent–Kung baby-step/giant-step chooses \(k\approx\sqrt n\):
\[
A(B)=\sum_q B^{qk}\left(\sum_{r<k}a_{qk+r}B^r\right).
\]
Precompute baby powers \(B^{r}\), form each block polynomial, then combine by Horner in \(B^{k}\). Merely forming every dense block as a separate linear combination can still cost \(O(n^2)\). The full Brent–Kung algorithm batches those combinations with rectangular matrix multiplication; its classical FFT bound is \(O((n\log n)^{3/2})\) field operations. Exact practical complexity and memory depend on the polynomial- and matrix-multiplication routines. The block decomposition is the conceptual step; it is not by itself a proof of an \(O(M(n)\sqrt n)\) implementation.
The condition \(B[0]=0\) is about information flow: \(B(x)^r\) then starts at degree \(r\), so a coefficient below \(n\) can only use \(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}\). With a nonzero constant term, arbitrarily high powers of \(B\) can influence the constant coefficient, so a finite prefix does not generally determine the composition.



For \(A(0)=0,A'(0)\ne0\), the linear coefficient is invertible, so there is one series \(B\) beginning with \(x/A'(0)\) that satisfies \(A(B)=x\). Newton solves the equation \(A(B)-x=0\) by the familiar tangent correction:
\[
B_{new}=B-\frac{A(B)-x}{A'(B)}\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\]
This needs composition plus multiplicative inversion and has the same asymptotic bottleneck as the chosen composition routine. If only one or a structured set of coefficients is needed, Lagrange inversion (chapter 08) is usually better:
For integers \(1\le k\le n\),
\[
[x^n]B(x)^k=\frac{k}{n}[t^{n-k}]\left(\frac{t}{A(t)}\right)^n.
\]
This divided form requires \(n\) to be invertible in the coefficient field; in small characteristic, use a division-free identity or a method designed for that characteristic.



Dense NTT is wasteful when only \(K\) coefficients of the defining series are nonzero. Coefficient recurrences from derivatives often give \(O(nK)\): for \(B=\exp(A)\), \(B'=A'B\), hence
\[
nb_n=\sum_{i=1}^n i a_i b_{n-i}.
\]
Similarly, after \(b_0=a_0^{-1}\), \(B=A^{-1}\) uses \(b_n=-a_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_{n-i}\) for \(n\ge1\). The exponential recurrence additionally divides by \(n\), so it is valid only while each \(1,\ldots,n\) is a unit (for example \(n<MOD\) over \(\mathbb F_{MOD}\)). Choose sparse versus dense by estimated work, not merely by degree.



Let \(A=1-x\). Then \(\operatorname{inv}(A) = 1+x+x^{2}+...\), \(\log(A)=-x-x^{2}/2-x^{3}/3-...\), and \(\operatorname{pow}(A,k)\) reproduces \(\sum_i(-1)^{i}{k\choose i}x^{i}\). This tiny example checks signs, integration inverses and truncation.
The point of the example is that every defining equation can be checked without knowing the implementation. When integrating these operations with your library, test algebraic identities on random small series:

\(A*\operatorname{inv}(A) = 1 \bmod x^{n}\);
\(\log(\exp(A)) = A\) when \(A[0]=0\);
\(\exp(\log(A)) = A\) when \(A[0]=1\);
\(\sqrt{A}^{2} = A\);
\(\operatorname{compose}(A,\operatorname{revert}(A)) = x\).

title: 07 — Formal Power Series
text:
Suppose \(B\) is an inverse approximation: \(AB\equiv1\pmod{x^{m}}\). The error \(E=1-AB\) has no terms below degree \(m\). Rather than solve missing coefficients individually, correct all of them in one multiplication: \[
B_{new}=B(2-AB)\pmod{x^{2m}}.
\] Indeed \(AB_{new}=AB(2-AB)=(1-E)(1+E)=1-E^2\). Thus the old error is squared; if \(E\) starts at degree \(m\), the new error starts at degree \(2m\). Precision doubles, and the total cost over lengths \(1,2,4,\ldots,n\) is \(O(M(n))\).
Precision doubling should operate on a truncated copy so that a caller’s longer series is not accidentally destroyed.

title: Suggested study plan
text:
This is a 24-week route at roughly 7–10 focused hours per week. Compress or expand it, but keep the dependency order and re-solve intervals. Hard problems matter more than finishing a calendar box.



Session A (90 min): derive the chapter’s main results by hand.
Session B (90 min): reproduce one key derivation, then solve a problem that requires recognizing or adapting it.
Sessions C/D (2–3 h each): one ordered problem per session. Record when each hint was opened.
Review (30 min): re-solve or verbally reconstruct one problem from two or six weeks earlier.

Stop a theory session when you can derive the result, state its preconditions, and explain which statement clues suggest it. Reading the same proof again is less valuable than deriving it on a blank page.

Capstones
Complete timed team-style attempts and postmortems.



Advanced sieves appear late because they are specialized and easier to retain after divisor inversion and interpolation are mature. If an imminent contest is known to favor number theory, move weeks 21–22 directly after week 7.



Keep each entry short enough that you will actually reread it:
Problem / date / time before first hint:
Recognition clue I missed:
Mathematical object and decisive identity:
Target complexity and why the naive form failed:
Implementation invariant or bug:
Re-solve dates (+14d, +42d):
Mastery means you can recover the solution from the first two lines after six weeks. Memorizing an editorial’s loop structure does not count.



During capstone weeks, use a three-person simulation even when practicing alone:

Spend 10 minutes producing only the mathematical model and complexity target.
Spend 10 minutes trying to falsify assumptions: prime modulus, invertibility, truncation degree, independence, overflow, and forgotten zero cases.
Only then implement. Write down which observations should be communicated to a teammate before coding starts.

For a real team, assign one person to derive, one to inspect algebraic contracts, and one to build a small oracle. Rotate these roles across problems.

title: 15 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
This chapter treats \(\mathbb F_p[x]\) the way Chapters 01–02 treat integers. Polynomials have degrees instead of absolute values, and a division algorithm replaces integer long division. Because coefficients lie in the field \(\mathbb F_p\), every nonzero leading coefficient is invertible: gcds, irreducibility, and factorization all behave cleanly. This is not true over a composite coefficient modulus.
The goal is to turn one polynomial into irreducible building blocks, just as integer factorization turns a number into primes. The standard pipeline is: remove repeated blocks, group the remaining blocks by degree, then split each same-degree group.


Normalize every nonzero gcd to monic (leading coefficient \(1\)), so the same mathematical gcd always has the same representation. Extended Euclid returns \(aA+bB=\gcd(A,B)\). Therefore \(A\) has an inverse modulo \(M\) exactly when \(\gcd(A,M)=1\): reduce the Bezout identity modulo \(M\). Modular polynomial exponentiation reduces after every multiplication, keeping degrees below \(\deg M\); it is the basic engine below.
For nonconstant \(f\), the quotient \(\mathbb F_p[x]/(f)\) is a field exactly when \(f\) is irreducible. If \(\deg f=d\), it has \(p^d\) elements, so every residue class \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\alpha^{p^d}=\alpha\). The map \(\alpha\mapsto\alpha^p\) is the Frobenius map; its repeated powers reveal factor degrees, replacing trial division by every possible polynomial.



Call \(f\) square-free if no irreducible factor is repeated. For \(f'\ne0\), \(\gcd(f,f')\) contains exactly the factors that occur more than once; repeated gcds and exact divisions separate factors by multiplicity. This must happen before the later stages, which assume distinct factors.
In characteristic \(p\), the derivative of \(x^{mp}\) is zero. Thus \(f'=0\) means every nonzero exponent is divisible by \(p\); over \(\mathbb F_p\) we can take the formal p-th root by dividing exponents by \(p\) and then recurse. Missing this branch is the classic finite-field factorization bug.



The polynomial \(x^{p^{d}}-x\) has precisely the elements of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\) as roots. Equivalently, it is the product of all monic irreducibles whose degree divides \(d\). Starting from \(h=x\), update \(h\leftarrow h^p\bmod f\); after \(d\) updates, \(h=x^{p^d}\bmod f\). Gcds with \(h-x\), after removing blocks found for smaller degrees, perform distinct-degree factorization: each remaining block is a product of irreducibles of one known degree.
For equal-degree factorization, Cantor–Zassenhaus chooses random \(a(x)\) and, for odd \(p\), splits with
\[\gcd\left(f,a^{(p^{d}-1)/2}-1\right).\]
Restart when the gcd is \(1\) or \(f\): the random choice did not distinguish the factors. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), use a trace-style sum rather than the half-order exponent. Berlekamp instead solves a linear-algebra problem for fixed points of Frobenius; for square-free \(f\), the relevant kernel dimension equals the number of irreducible factors. It is a useful deterministic alternative for small fields, while Cantor–Zassenhaus is often simpler for a large prime field.



Linear factors are \(\gcd(f,x^{p}-x)\), because \(x^p-x\) vanishes on exactly the \(p\) field elements. Factor that square-free component to list roots. Return roots with multiplicities only after square-free decomposition. For every randomized algorithm, the final certificate is deterministic: multiply the monic factors, restore multiplicities, and compare with the monic input.




Coefficients lie in a prime field; composite coefficient moduli invalidate division.
Keep polynomials trimmed and gcds monic.
Polynomial modular exponentiation must reduce degrees after every multiply.
Random splitters need independent retries and a deterministic reconstruction check.

title: 15 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Normalize every nonzero gcd to monic (leading coefficient \(1\)), so the same mathematical gcd always has the same representation. Extended Euclid returns \(aA+bB=\gcd(A,B)\). Therefore \(A\) has an inverse modulo \(M\) exactly when \(\gcd(A,M)=1\): reduce the Bezout identity modulo \(M\). Modular polynomial exponentiation reduces after every multiplication, keeping degrees below \(\deg M\); it is the basic engine below.
For nonconstant \(f\), the quotient \(\mathbb F_p[x]/(f)\) is a field exactly when \(f\) is irreducible. If \(\deg f=d\), it has \(p^d\) elements, so every residue class \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\alpha^{p^d}=\alpha\). The map \(\alpha\mapsto\alpha^p\) is the Frobenius map; its repeated powers reveal factor degrees, replacing trial division by every possible polynomial.

title: 15 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Call \(f\) square-free if no irreducible factor is repeated. For \(f'\ne0\), \(\gcd(f,f')\) contains exactly the factors that occur more than once; repeated gcds and exact divisions separate factors by multiplicity. This must happen before the later stages, which assume distinct factors.
In characteristic \(p\), the derivative of \(x^{mp}\) is zero. Thus \(f'=0\) means every nonzero exponent is divisible by \(p\); over \(\mathbb F_p\) we can take the formal p-th root by dividing exponents by \(p\) and then recurse. Missing this branch is the classic finite-field factorization bug.

title: 15 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
The polynomial \(x^{p^{d}}-x\) has precisely the elements of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\) as roots. Equivalently, it is the product of all monic irreducibles whose degree divides \(d\). Starting from \(h=x\), update \(h\leftarrow h^p\bmod f\); after \(d\) updates, \(h=x^{p^d}\bmod f\). Gcds with \(h-x\), after removing blocks found for smaller degrees, perform distinct-degree factorization: each remaining block is a product of irreducibles of one known degree.
For equal-degree factorization, Cantor–Zassenhaus chooses random \(a(x)\) and, for odd \(p\), splits with
\[\gcd\left(f,a^{(p^{d}-1)/2}-1\right).\]
Restart when the gcd is \(1\) or \(f\): the random choice did not distinguish the factors. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), use a trace-style sum rather than the half-order exponent. Berlekamp instead solves a linear-algebra problem for fixed points of Frobenius; for square-free \(f\), the relevant kernel dimension equals the number of irreducible factors. It is a useful deterministic alternative for small fields, while Cantor–Zassenhaus is often simpler for a large prime field.

title: 15 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text: Linear factors are \(\gcd(f,x^{p}-x)\), because \(x^p-x\) vanishes on exactly the \(p\) field elements. Factor that square-free component to list roots. Return roots with multiplicities only after square-free decomposition. For every randomized algorithm, the final certificate is deterministic: multiply the monic factors, restore multiplicities, and compare with the monic input.
