title: 18 — Holonomic (D-Finite and P-Recursive) Methods
text:
The linear recurrences in Chapter 10 have constant coefficients. They describe sequences such as Fibonacci where the same multiplier is used at every index. Many combinatorial sequences need multipliers that depend polynomially on the index instead. A sequence is P-recursive when
\[\sum_{j=0}^{r}P_j(n)a_{n-j}=0\]
for fixed polynomials \(P_j\) (after a finite set of initial indices). Over characteristic zero, this is equivalent to its ordinary generating function being D-finite: it obeys a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients. This broader class captures many binomial sums, diagonals, walks, and labelled graph counts. Classical closure theorems are stated in characteristic zero. Computing a derived recurrence modulo a prime is safe only after tracking denominators and separately handling indices where they vanish.


The bridge is coefficient extraction. If \(F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n\), then
\[xF'(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}n a_nx^n.\]
Repeated derivatives supply falling-factorial polynomials in \(n\), and a factor \(x^i\) shifts the coefficient index. Therefore a differential equation converts mechanically to a P-recurrence, and conversely.
For a concrete example, the central binomial coefficients satisfy
\[ (n+1)a_{n+1}=2(2n+1)a_n,\qquad a_0=1. \]
Their OGF \(F(x)=(1-4x)^{-1/2}\) satisfies \((1-4x)F'(x)-2F(x)=0\). Either description determines the same sequence, but the differential equation is often easier to derive from a generating-function model. Keep enough initial terms and separately handle indices where the leading polynomial vanishes.



D-finite series are closed under addition, multiplication, differentiation, integration, composition with an algebraic series having zero constant term, and diagonal extraction. Every algebraic series is D-finite, but \(\exp(\exp x)\) is a standard warning that arbitrary composition is not closed. Thus closure is a proof tool, not a licence to compose any two familiar functions. Multiple sums of hypergeometric terms are strong candidates for creative telescoping and P-recursiveness.
Useful contest workflow:

derive an OGF/EGF or a fixed-dimensional binomial sum;
prove it lies in a closed D-finite class;
derive the differential equation symbolically, or guess a bounded-order and bounded-degree recurrence from exact terms;
certify the guessed relation algebraically—sample agreement is not proof;
evaluate with the recurrence, treating singular indices explicitly.




For assumed order \(r\) and coefficient degree \(d\), solve a homogeneous linear system for \((r+1)(d+1)\) unknown coefficients using more exact sequence terms than unknowns. Verifying on unused terms is a valuable bug check, not a proof: the guessed relation must still follow from the original expression, a differential equation, or a certified creative-telescoping identity. This practical route is sometimes called “Min25-BM,” though the recurrence has polynomial rather than constant coefficients.
A fixed-order P-recurrence is a product of companion matrices whose entries are rational functions of \(n\). Direct evaluation is linear in \(N\) and is usually the right first implementation. For a very distant coefficient, baby-step/ giant-step polynomial matrix products plus fast multipoint shift can obtain it in \(\widetilde O(\sqrt N)\) field operations for fixed order and degree, subject to nonvanishing denominators; the hidden logarithmic factors depend on the polynomial-multiplication and shift routines.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
This chapter is about changing the indexing of a sum: from integers to prime powers, from pairs to their gcd, or from every quotient to the \(O(\sqrt n)\) distinct values of \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\). The formulas are less important than the objects they regroup. Each section says what a new coordinate represents, so that it can be re-derived when the statement changes slightly.


Factorization is useful because most arithmetic functions are determined by a number’s prime powers. Trial division asks every small prime whether it divides \(n\), which becomes too slow for large 64-bit inputs. For arbitrary unsigned 64-bit integers, use deterministic Miller–Rabin to tell primes from composites and Pollard–Rho to split composites.


For odd \(n\), write \(n-1=d\cdot2^{s}\) with \(d\) odd. If \(n\) is prime and \(a\not\equiv0\pmod n\), set \(x=a^d\). Because \(x^{2^s}=1\) and a field has only the two square roots \(\pm1\) of \(1\), the squaring chain must either start at \(1\) or reach \(-1\) before it reaches \(1\). A base that does neither is a witness that \(n\) is composite. A base that passes is only evidence, which is why several bases are tested. After handling \(n<4\) and reducing every base modulo \(n\), testing bases
\({2, 325, 9375, 28178, 450775, 9780504, 1795265022}\)
is deterministic for all 64-bit inputs. Complexity is \(O(\log n)\) modular multiplications per base.



Iterate a pseudo-random polynomial \(f(x)=x²+c \bmod n\). Although the sequence is not visibly periodic modulo \(n\), it eventually cycles modulo an unknown factor \(p\). If two iterates \(x,y\) agree modulo \(p\), then \(p\mid(x-y)\), and \(\gcd(|x-y|,n)\) can reveal a nontrivial divisor without knowing \(p\) first. Floyd/Brent cycle detection and batched gcds make this fast in practice. It is randomized with heuristic expected time about \(O(p^{1/2})\) for a factor \(p\), often described as \(O(n^{1/4})\) for balanced semiprimes.
Pitfalls. Handle \(n<2\); use unsigned 128-bit multiplication; restart Rho when it returns \(n\); recursion receives prime powers as well as semiprimes; randomized runtime has no strict worst-case guarantee.




\(f\) is multiplicative when \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(ab)=f(a)f(b)\) for coprime \(a,b\). Prime factorization then says that \(f(n)\) is the product of its values on the prime-power factors of \(n\). It does not say \(f(ab)=f(a)f(b)\) when \(a,b\) share a prime. For example \(\varphi(2)\varphi(2)=1\) but \(\varphi(4)=2\). Central examples are:



\(f(n)\)
prime-power value \(f(p^{e})\)
interpretation




\(\varphi\)
\(p^{e}-p^{e-1}\)
units modulo \(n\)


\(\mu\)
\(-1\) if \(e=1\), else \(0\)
inverse of constant-one function


\(τ\)
\(e+1\)
number of divisors


\(\sigma_k\)
\(1+p^{k}+…+p^{ek}\)
sum of kth powers of divisors



The Euler/linear sieve visits each composite exactly once as \(i\cdot p\), where \(p\) is its least prime factor. The “stop when \(p\) divides \(i\)” rule is what makes that representation unique. Keep enough information about the exponent of the least prime to distinguish, for example, whether adding another \(p\) makes \(\mu\) zero or changes \(\varphi(p^e)\) to \(\varphi(p^{e+1})\). It computes primes, \(\mu\), and \(\varphi\) through \(N\) in \(O(N)\) time and memory.



For arithmetic functions, Dirichlet convolution combines two functions by splitting an integer into an ordered pair of divisors:
\[ (f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n} f(d)g(n/d). \]
For example \((1*1)(6)\) counts the divisors of \(6\), because each divisor \(d\) chooses the factorization \(6=d\cdot(6/d)\). It is associative and commutative, with identity \(ε(1)=1\), \(ε(n>1)=0\). Convolution preserves multiplicativity. Let \(1(n)=1\); since \(1*\mu=ε\),
\[F(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)F(n/d).\]
This is not a formula to memorize in isolation. \(F(n)\) is the sum of \(f\) over divisors of \(n\), so it says \(F=f*1\); convolving both sides with \(\mu\) cancels \(1\) and recovers \(f\). Useful identities follow immediately:
\[1*\varphi=\operatorname{id},\qquad \mu*\operatorname{id}=\varphi,
\qquad 1*1=\tau.\]


If a condition asks for \(\gcd(x,y)=1\), the following identity is a filter:
\[[\gcd(x,y)=1]=\sum_{d\mid x,\ d\mid y}\mu(d).\]
Why does it work? If \(g=\gcd(x,y)\), the right side is \(\sum_{d\mid g}\mu(d)\), which is \(1\) when \(g=1\) and \(0\) otherwise. The pair sum becomes \(\sum_d \mu(d) A_d B_d\), where \(A_d,B_d\) count multiples of \(d\). More generally, group pairs by their gcd, derive a divisor zeta relation, then invert.




For arrays on \([1,N]\), the divisor zeta transform replaces the value at \(j\) by the sum of values stored at its divisors: \(F[j]=\sum_{d\mid j}f[d]\). Direct non-in-place divisor loops cost \(N(1+1/2+\cdots+1/N)=O(N\log N)\); inversion follows from the arithmetic Möbius formula. Prime-wise in-place updates compute the transform and its inverse in \(O(N\log\log N)\). For each prime \(p\), the divisor-zeta update \(f[ip]\mathrel{+}=f[i]\) for \(ip\le N\) must traverse \(i\) upward so prime powers accumulate; its inverse uses the same pairs in downward \(i\) order while subtracting. For example, the \(p=2\) stage sends the contribution at \(1\) first to \(2\), then that accumulated contribution to \(4\). After a set of prime stages, the value at \(x\) has accumulated exactly the divisors obtained by lowering the exponents of those primes; this is the no-overcounting invariant. The multiple zeta transform \(F[d]=\sum_{d\mid j}f[j]\) reverses the divisibility order: for each prime \(p\), apply \(f[i]\mathrel{+}=f[ip]\) with \(i\) decreasing, and invert with subtraction while \(i\) increases. Divisor zeta diagonalizes LCM convolution, while multiple zeta diagonalizes GCD convolution; the more general poset view appears in the transforms chapter.
The word “diagonalizes” is a double count. If \(h[x]=\sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=x}f[a]g[b]\), then
\[
\sum_{d\mid x}h[d]
=\sum_{a\mid x}\sum_{b\mid x}f[a]g[b]
=F[x]G[x].
\]
The first equality holds because \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\mid x\) exactly when both \(a\mid x\) and \(b\mid x\). Reversing all divisibility signs gives the same proof for GCD convolution and the multiple transform.
Example. If \(f[1]=2,f[2]=3,f[3]=5\), then the transformed value at \(6\) is \(f[1]+f[2]+f[3]+f[6]\). This is the integer analogue of a subset zeta transform: “submask” becomes “divisor.” Recognition. If every operation replaces a set by all divisors, every query involves \(\gcd\), or values are bounded while query count is large, transform the entire frequency vector instead of processing elements individually.



The value \(q=\lfloor n/l\rfloor\) does not change one index at a time. Once it has value \(q\), it remains constant through
\[r=\left\lfloor n/q\right\rfloor.\]
This works because \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor=q\) exactly when \(n/(q+1)<i\le n/q\). Thus a loop for (l=1; l<=n; l=r+1) has only \(O(\sqrt n)\) iterations. The distinct quotients are precisely the small integers up to \(\sqrt n\) plus values \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) for small \(i\).
For two or more floor terms, take the minimum end point: if a summand uses \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) and \(\lfloor m/i\rfloor\), then compute the end point for each nonzero current quotient and take their minimum. If the loop continues beyond one numerator, that quotient is zero and remains zero through the loop’s final bound; do not evaluate m/(m/l) when m/l is zero. Pair this with prefix sums of \(\mu\), \(\varphi\), powers, or another arithmetic function.
A standard derivation is
\[\sum_{i=1}^n \left\lfloor\frac ni\right\rfloor
=\sum_{ab\le n}1=\sum_{k\le n}\tau(k),\]
showing how a floor sum and a divisor sum are the same lattice-point count.



If \(f(1)≠0\) in a coefficient field, its Dirichlet inverse is the function \(g\) for which \(f*g=ε\). The \(n=1\) equation fixes \(g(1)\); every larger \(n\) equation has exactly one unknown term, \(f(1)g(n)\), giving the recurrence
\[g(1)=1/f(1),\qquad
g(n)=-\frac1{f(1)}\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\d>1}}f(d)g(n/d).\]
In prefix-sum problems, search for an easy convolution identity \(f*g=h\). Summing for \(n≤N\) and swapping divisors yields
\[\sum_{n\le N}h(n)=\sum_{d\le N}f(d)\,G(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If the \(d=1\) term contains the unknown prefix \(G(N)\), isolate it. Quotient grouping then turns the rest into \(O(\sqrt{N})\) states. This is the bridge to Du Jiao sieve in Chapter 03.



The Gaussian integers \(\mathbb Z[i]\) are numbers \(a+bi\) with integer coordinates. Their norm \(N(a+bi)=a^{2}+b^{2}\) is nonnegative and, crucially, multiplicative: \(N(zw)=N(z)N(w)\). They admit Euclidean division by rounding a complex quotient to nearby integer coordinates. Hence gcd, units, associates, and unique factorization behave much like the integers. Use exact integer arithmetic to test the few rounding candidates; floating point may select the wrong quotient for large coordinates.
For a positive integer \(n\), Fermat’s two-square theorem says \(n\) is a sum of two squares iff every prime \(p=3 \bmod 4\) has even exponent. For \(p=1 \bmod 4\), find a square root of \(-1 \bmod p\) and run Cornacchia/Euclidean descent to obtain \(p=x^{2}+y^{2}\). The local representation of \(p^e\) is then \((x+yi)^e\): it is important to raise the Gaussian integer, not merely the integer coordinates. The other local cases are explicit: \(2^e=N((1+i)^e)\), and a \(3\bmod4\) prime with exponent \(2e\) contributes \(p^{2e}=(p^e)^2+0^2\). Multiply local representations with
\[ (a^{2}+b^{2})(c^{2}+d^{2})=(ac-bd)^{2}+(ad+bc)^{2}, \]
Normalize signs/order only after constructing the result.




Multiplicative is not completely multiplicative: \(\varphi(p²)≠\varphi(p)²\).
Decide whether a divisor formula uses \(f(d)\) or \(f(n/d)\) before coding.
\(\mu(n)=0\) whenever a square divides \(n\).
Frequency transforms require a bounded value domain; factorization-based inclusion–exclusion may be better for sparse large values.
Quotient blocks must use 64-bit division; for multiple floors, update the end point for each one.
Pollard–Rho factor lists contain repetitions; compress them before enumerating divisors or inclusion–exclusion subsets.

text:
For arithmetic functions, Dirichlet convolution combines two functions by splitting an integer into an ordered pair of divisors:
\[ (f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n} f(d)g(n/d). \]
For example \((1*1)(6)\) counts the divisors of \(6\), because each divisor \(d\) chooses the factorization \(6=d\cdot(6/d)\). It is associative and commutative, with identity \(ε(1)=1\), \(ε(n>1)=0\). Convolution preserves multiplicativity. Let \(1(n)=1\); since \(1*\mu=ε\),
\[F(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)F(n/d).\]
This is not a formula to memorize in isolation. \(F(n)\) is the sum of \(f\) over divisors of \(n\), so it says \(F=f*1\); convolving both sides with \(\mu\) cancels \(1\) and recovers \(f\). Useful identities follow immediately:
\[1*\varphi=\operatorname{id},\qquad \mu*\operatorname{id}=\varphi,
\qquad 1*1=\tau.\]


If a condition asks for \(\gcd(x,y)=1\), the following identity is a filter:
\[[\gcd(x,y)=1]=\sum_{d\mid x,\ d\mid y}\mu(d).\]
Why does it work? If \(g=\gcd(x,y)\), the right side is \(\sum_{d\mid g}\mu(d)\), which is \(1\) when \(g=1\) and \(0\) otherwise. The pair sum becomes \(\sum_d \mu(d) A_d B_d\), where \(A_d,B_d\) count multiples of \(d\). More generally, group pairs by their gcd, derive a divisor zeta relation, then invert.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
For arrays on \([1,N]\), the divisor zeta transform replaces the value at \(j\) by the sum of values stored at its divisors: \(F[j]=\sum_{d\mid j}f[d]\). Direct non-in-place divisor loops cost \(N(1+1/2+\cdots+1/N)=O(N\log N)\); inversion follows from the arithmetic Möbius formula. Prime-wise in-place updates compute the transform and its inverse in \(O(N\log\log N)\). For each prime \(p\), the divisor-zeta update \(f[ip]\mathrel{+}=f[i]\) for \(ip\le N\) must traverse \(i\) upward so prime powers accumulate; its inverse uses the same pairs in downward \(i\) order while subtracting. For example, the \(p=2\) stage sends the contribution at \(1\) first to \(2\), then that accumulated contribution to \(4\). After a set of prime stages, the value at \(x\) has accumulated exactly the divisors obtained by lowering the exponents of those primes; this is the no-overcounting invariant. The multiple zeta transform \(F[d]=\sum_{d\mid j}f[j]\) reverses the divisibility order: for each prime \(p\), apply \(f[i]\mathrel{+}=f[ip]\) with \(i\) decreasing, and invert with subtraction while \(i\) increases. Divisor zeta diagonalizes LCM convolution, while multiple zeta diagonalizes GCD convolution; the more general poset view appears in the transforms chapter.
The word “diagonalizes” is a double count. If \(h[x]=\sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=x}f[a]g[b]\), then
\[
\sum_{d\mid x}h[d]
=\sum_{a\mid x}\sum_{b\mid x}f[a]g[b]
=F[x]G[x].
\]
The first equality holds because \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\mid x\) exactly when both \(a\mid x\) and \(b\mid x\). Reversing all divisibility signs gives the same proof for GCD convolution and the multiple transform.
Example. If \(f[1]=2,f[2]=3,f[3]=5\), then the transformed value at \(6\) is \(f[1]+f[2]+f[3]+f[6]\). This is the integer analogue of a subset zeta transform: “submask” becomes “divisor.” Recognition. If every operation replaces a set by all divisors, every query involves \(\gcd\), or values are bounded while query count is large, transform the entire frequency vector instead of processing elements individually.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
The value \(q=\lfloor n/l\rfloor\) does not change one index at a time. Once it has value \(q\), it remains constant through
\[r=\left\lfloor n/q\right\rfloor.\]
This works because \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor=q\) exactly when \(n/(q+1)<i\le n/q\). Thus a loop for (l=1; l<=n; l=r+1) has only \(O(\sqrt n)\) iterations. The distinct quotients are precisely the small integers up to \(\sqrt n\) plus values \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) for small \(i\).
For two or more floor terms, take the minimum end point: if a summand uses \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) and \(\lfloor m/i\rfloor\), then compute the end point for each nonzero current quotient and take their minimum. If the loop continues beyond one numerator, that quotient is zero and remains zero through the loop’s final bound; do not evaluate m/(m/l) when m/l is zero. Pair this with prefix sums of \(\mu\), \(\varphi\), powers, or another arithmetic function.
A standard derivation is
\[\sum_{i=1}^n \left\lfloor\frac ni\right\rfloor
=\sum_{ab\le n}1=\sum_{k\le n}\tau(k),\]
showing how a floor sum and a divisor sum are the same lattice-point count.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
If \(f(1)≠0\) in a coefficient field, its Dirichlet inverse is the function \(g\) for which \(f*g=ε\). The \(n=1\) equation fixes \(g(1)\); every larger \(n\) equation has exactly one unknown term, \(f(1)g(n)\), giving the recurrence
\[g(1)=1/f(1),\qquad
g(n)=-\frac1{f(1)}\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\d>1}}f(d)g(n/d).\]
In prefix-sum problems, search for an easy convolution identity \(f*g=h\). Summing for \(n≤N\) and swapping divisors yields
\[\sum_{n\le N}h(n)=\sum_{d\le N}f(d)\,G(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If the \(d=1\) term contains the unknown prefix \(G(N)\), isolate it. Quotient grouping then turns the rest into \(O(\sqrt{N})\) states. This is the bridge to Du Jiao sieve in Chapter 03.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
The Gaussian integers \(\mathbb Z[i]\) are numbers \(a+bi\) with integer coordinates. Their norm \(N(a+bi)=a^{2}+b^{2}\) is nonnegative and, crucially, multiplicative: \(N(zw)=N(z)N(w)\). They admit Euclidean division by rounding a complex quotient to nearby integer coordinates. Hence gcd, units, associates, and unique factorization behave much like the integers. Use exact integer arithmetic to test the few rounding candidates; floating point may select the wrong quotient for large coordinates.
For a positive integer \(n\), Fermat’s two-square theorem says \(n\) is a sum of two squares iff every prime \(p=3 \bmod 4\) has even exponent. For \(p=1 \bmod 4\), find a square root of \(-1 \bmod p\) and run Cornacchia/Euclidean descent to obtain \(p=x^{2}+y^{2}\). The local representation of \(p^e\) is then \((x+yi)^e\): it is important to raise the Gaussian integer, not merely the integer coordinates. The other local cases are explicit: \(2^e=N((1+i)^e)\), and a \(3\bmod4\) prime with exponent \(2e\) contributes \(p^{2e}=(p^e)^2+0^2\). Multiply local representations with
\[ (a^{2}+b^{2})(c^{2}+d^{2})=(ac-bd)^{2}+(ad+bc)^{2}, \]
Normalize signs/order only after constructing the result.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Multiplicative is not completely multiplicative: \(\varphi(p²)≠\varphi(p)²\).
Decide whether a divisor formula uses \(f(d)\) or \(f(n/d)\) before coding.
\(\mu(n)=0\) whenever a square divides \(n\).
Frequency transforms require a bounded value domain; factorization-based inclusion–exclusion may be better for sparse large values.
Quotient blocks must use 64-bit division; for multiple floors, update the end point for each one.
Pollard–Rho factor lists contain repetitions; compress them before enumerating divisors or inclusion–exclusion subsets.

title: Advanced Mathematics for ICPC
text:
Build the recognition, derivation, and modelling skills behind hard competitive-programming mathematics. The course assumes you already have a tested implementation library and focuses on deciding what to apply and why it works.
Start with the prerequisite audit or open the study plan.
This is a dependency-guided course for an experienced competitive programmer who already solves around Codeforces 2200 level. It is deliberately biased toward techniques that turn a difficult mathematical observation into an implementable algorithm. Geometry is out of scope.
The notes assume that the reader already has a comprehensive, tested algorithm library. They focus on contracts, derivations, recognition clues, and failure modes rather than reproducing standard implementations. Code appears only when a non-standard snippet materially clarifies an idea. Shared symbols and preconditions are collected in notation reference.

title: Advanced Mathematics for ICPC
text:
How to use the course

Take the prerequisite audit. Patch only the gaps it exposes.
Read a chapter’s theory before opening its problem hints.
Attempt each problem for 60–120 minutes. Open Hint 1 only when you cannot name the relevant mathematical object; open Hint 2 only when the reduction remains unclear; use Hint 3 when you know the mathematics but cannot obtain the target complexity.
After solving, write a three-line postmortem: recognition clue, decisive identity, and the implementation hazard you would miss next time.
Re-solve Mastery and Capstone problems after two and six weeks.

For a concrete multi-month cadence, use the optional 24-week study plan.
Problem levels used throughout the repository are local to this course:

Foundation isolates one prerequisite or modelling step.
Advanced combines a central theorem with a standard algorithm.
Mastery hides the model or requires a non-obvious transformation.
Capstone combines several chapters or is appropriate team-contest work.

title: Advanced Mathematics for ICPC
text:
Source and spoiler policy
Statements are linked, not copied. The notes paraphrase the mathematical idea and give layered hints rather than complete solutions to listed exercises. Official statements and editorials are preferred; high-quality community tutorials are used where they explain a theorem better. A language label is shown when a useful source is not English. See the sources page for the source hierarchy and durable reference material.
No collection can guarantee that a future ICPC problem will not introduce new mathematics. The goal here is stronger and more realistic: build the common toolkit, the habit of deriving missing variants, and enough hard practice that a new statement can be reduced to familiar algebra under contest pressure.

title: Notation and algebra contracts
text:
The same symbol can denote very different operations in contest editorials. These notes use the following conventions unless a chapter overrides them.



\([x^{n}]F(x)\) is the coefficient of \(x^{n}\).
\(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) is the ring of residues modulo \(m\).
\(\mathbb F_p\) is a field only when \(p\) is prime.
mint denotes a modular-integer type whose modulus is stated nearby.
Division by \(a\) means multiplication by \(a^{-1}\) and therefore requires that \(a\) be a unit. In \(\mathbb F_p\) this is equivalent to \(a\ne0\); modulo a composite \(m\) it is equivalent to \(\gcd(a,m)=1\).
For nonzero \(n\), \(v_p(n)\) is the exponent of prime \(p\) in \(n\); when needed, \(v_p(0)=+\infty\).





\(\mathbf 1(n)=1\), \(\varepsilon(1)=1\) and \(\varepsilon(n)=0\) for \(n>1\).
\(\mu\), \(\varphi\), and \(\tau\) are the Möbius, Euler-totient, and divisor-count functions.
Dirichlet convolution is \((f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)g(n/d)\); its identity is \(\varepsilon\).
A function is multiplicative when \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(ab)=f(a)f(b)\) for \(\gcd(a,b)=1\); “completely multiplicative” drops the coprimality requirement.





Polynomials and formal power series are coefficient arrays in increasing degree order.
\(F\bmod x^{n}\) means retain degrees \(0,\ldots,n-1\).
Multiplicative inverse \(F^{-1}\) requires \(F(0)\) to be a unit.
Formal \(\log F\) is normalized to constant term zero and normally requires \(F(0)=1\); formal \(\exp F\) normally requires \(F(0)=0\).
Formal composition \(F(G(x))\) is automatically well-defined for arbitrary infinite FPS only when \(G(0)=0\). Truncated or polynomial cases may allow more.
Compositional inverse/reversion requires \(F(0)=0\) and \(F'(0)\) a unit.
NTT length and root-of-unity conditions are part of an algorithm’s contract, not implementation trivia.
\(\binom nr_q\) is a Gaussian/q-binomial coefficient; the subscript is a numerical field size or formal variable, not the arithmetic modulus.
A set power series has coefficients \(F[S]\) and multiplication \((FG)[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}F[T]G[S\setminus T]\).
\(F^{(j)}\) denotes the \(j\)th formal derivative; in a set-series chapter a partial derivative with respect to an element variable is named explicitly.





\(\operatorname{Pf}(A)\) is the Pfaffian of an even skew-symmetric matrix; over characteristic other than two, \(\operatorname{Pf}(A)^{2}=\det A\).
\(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) is the adjugate and satisfies \(A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I\) even when \(A\) is singular.
A P-recursive sequence satisfies a fixed-order recurrence with polynomial coefficients in the index. A D-finite series satisfies a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients.
Classical D-finite closure statements are characteristic-zero results. Modular computation requires checking every denominator and singular index.





Subsets are bitmasks when the ground set is \([0,n)\).
The subset zeta transform sends \(f(S)\) to \(\sum_{T\subseteq S}f(T)\).
XOR/AND/OR convolution names refer to the operation combining indices, not the pointwise operation after transformation.
“Möbius inversion” may mean inversion on subsets, the divisor poset, or a general locally finite poset. The chapter always names the order relation.





\(M(n)\) denotes the cost of multiplying degree-below-\(n\) polynomials; with a suitable NTT, \(M(n)=O(n\log n)\).
A bound such as \(O(M(n))\) can conceal a large constant and strict modulus requirements. Use the actual maximum degree and transform count when judging feasibility.
Randomized algorithms state whether their guarantee is Las Vegas (always correct, random time) or Monte Carlo (small error probability).





Signed overflow is never intentional. Products near the 64-bit boundary use __int128 or an explicitly justified unsigned technique.
Routine algorithms are assumed to come from the reader’s tested library; the notes state the contracts and arithmetic assumptions needed to select them.

title: 11 — Probability and Expectation
text:
Competitive-programming probability is usually deterministic algebra wearing a random story. First say what is random and what is fixed, then define a state, write a one-step equation, and solve the resulting DAG, linear system, or generating function. A probability formula is useful only once its events are unambiguous.


For an event \(A\), let \(I_A=[A]\) be 1 when it occurs and 0 otherwise. Its average is therefore \(E[I_A]=P(A)\). If a quantity is a count, try to express it as a sum of one indicator per possible contribution:
\[X=\sum_i [A_i],\qquad E[X]=\sum_iP(A_i),\]
whether the events are independent is irrelevant. We use only distributivity of expectation over addition, not a product rule. This is the first tool for expected inversions, occupied boxes, surviving edges, and distinct values.
Worked example. In a uniformly random permutation of \(n\) items, each pair is inverted with probability \(1/2\). Hence the expected inversion count is \(\binom n2/2\), without describing any transition process.
For products, independence does matter: \(E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]\) is not generally true. Condition instead when dependence is awkward.



Partition outcomes by the next random choice. The events \(Y=y\) are disjoint and cover all outcomes, so averaging in two stages gives
\[E[X]=\sum_y P(Y=y)E[X\mid Y=y].\]
The common self-loop pattern comes from an action that leaves the state unchanged with probability \(p\), while the other outcomes have probabilities \(q_i\) with \(p+\sum_iq_i=1\):
\[E=s+pE+\sum_iq_iE_i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E=\frac{s+\sum_iq_iE_i}{1-p}.\]
The numerator is the immediate cost plus the expected cost after a genuine state change; division conditions on eventually leaving the self-loop. Never implement an iterative self-reference before algebraically removing it. If \(p=1\) in a nonterminal state whose target can be reached only after leaving, the target is unreachable and the hitting expectation is infinite.
For a fair die that is rerolled until it shows \(4,5,\) or \(6\), one roll costs one and fails with probability \(1/2\). Thus \(E=1+E/2\), so \(E=2\). The division does not assume that attempts are bounded; it sums the entire self-loop tail.
Conditioning can also reduce state: reveal the first special object, the maximum sampled index, or the number of successful trials—whatever makes the remaining process symmetric.



Two equivalent state choices are common. Choose the one whose transition is easier to state and whose terminal condition is obvious:

p[state]: probability of reaching the state; push mass forward and sum terminal rewards.
E[state]: expected remaining cost; pull from successor expectations.

Use probability mass for acyclic processes and distributions; use expectation states when only one moment is needed. State aggregation is the hard part. Two histories may be merged only when they have the same distribution of future outcomes. Exchangeable objects should be represented by counts, not identities: e.g. \((c1,c2,c3)\) plates containing 1, 2, or 3 sushi. The plate labels do not affect a future random choice, but the counts do.
If transitions strictly increase/decrease a measure, topologically order states. Otherwise you have cycles and need equations.



Partition a finite Markov chain into transient states and absorbing states. A transient state may be revisited; an absorbing state, once entered, remains forever:
\[P=\begin{pmatrix}Q&R\\0&I\end{pmatrix}.\]
Starting from a transient state costs one step, then moves according to \(Q\). Writing that first-step equation simultaneously for all states gives expected hitting times
\[t=\mathbf1+Qt,\qquad (I-Q)t=\mathbf1.\]
For absorption in a chosen target class, the probability vector satisfies \((I-Q)h=Rb\), where \(b\) is \(1\) on target absorbing states and \(0\) on the other absorbing states. The fundamental matrix \(N=(I-Q)^{-1}=I+Q+Q^2+\cdots\) has N[i][j] equal to the expected number of visits to transient state \(j\) starting at \(i\), counting the initial visit when \(i=j\): \(Q^r\) records being there after \(r\) transitions.
You do not normally invert a matrix explicitly: solve linear systems. Dense cost is \(O(S^3)\). Exploit banded, tridiagonal, monotone, or graph structure. For a finite chain, the hitting time of the chosen absorbing set has finite expectation precisely when that set is reached with probability one from the start state. Reaching some other absorbing class does not count as success.



For a nonnegative integer-valued random variable \(X\), the probability generating function stores the whole distribution as coefficients:
\[G_X(z)=E[z^{X}]=\sum_kP(X=k)z^{k}.\]
Independent sums multiply PGFs because \(z^{X+Y}=z^Xz^Y\) and expectation of a product factors under independence. Moreover \(G'_X(1)=E[X]\) and \(G''_X(1)=E[X(X-1)]\) when those moments are finite, so
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=G''_X(1)+G'_X(1)-G'_X(1)^2.\]
This turns repeated independent dice/steps into polynomial multiplication.
First-step recurrences translate into rational GFs. For a renewal process with step PGF \(A(z)\), geometric repetition often produces \(1/(1-A(z))\). This connects probability DP to formal power series and linear recurrences.




“Uniformly select an available action” changes probabilities as the state changes.
Expected ratio is not ratio of expectations.
Modulo probabilities require all denominators invertible; this evaluates the same rational equations in a field, but field values have no ordering and do not make an infinite real expectation finite.
For double, use pivoting in cyclic systems and avoid subtracting nearly equal probabilities.
An unreachable absorbing state means infinite expectation, not a large finite DP value.
Memoized recursion on a cyclic state graph never resolves the cycle.

title: 11 — Probability and Expectation
text:
For an event \(A\), let \(I_A=[A]\) be 1 when it occurs and 0 otherwise. Its average is therefore \(E[I_A]=P(A)\). If a quantity is a count, try to express it as a sum of one indicator per possible contribution:
\[X=\sum_i [A_i],\qquad E[X]=\sum_iP(A_i),\]
whether the events are independent is irrelevant. We use only distributivity of expectation over addition, not a product rule. This is the first tool for expected inversions, occupied boxes, surviving edges, and distinct values.
Worked example. In a uniformly random permutation of \(n\) items, each pair is inverted with probability \(1/2\). Hence the expected inversion count is \(\binom n2/2\), without describing any transition process.

title: Prerequisite audit
text:
This is a gate, not a chapter. Work without references and mark an item weak if you cannot state both a correct algorithm and its preconditions in ten minutes. The advanced chapters assume at least 80% confidence here.



Prove Bézout’s identity implies the modular-inverse criterion \(\gcd(a,m)=1\), including the non-coprime linear-congruence case.
Derive the ordinary and generalized CRT merge for two congruences, including the inconsistency condition.
Explain why Fermat division fails under a composite modulus.
Compute \(v_p(n!)\) and derive \(\binom nk \bmod p\) with factorials for \(n<p\).
Derive the linear sieve invariant: each composite is visited at its least prime factor.
Switch freely between a recurrence, a DP transition, and a coefficient of a product of polynomials.
Use inclusion–exclusion and Möbius inversion on the divisor lattice in their basic forms.
Perform Gaussian elimination over a prime field and distinguish no, one, and many solutions.
Apply linearity of expectation without assuming independence.





State the overflow boundaries of modular arithmetic and __int128.
Recognize binary exponentiation as a monoid operation, not only an integer routine.
State the contracts of factorial tables, sieves, and matrix exponentiation.
Design randomized tests against an \(O(n^{2})\) or exhaustive oracle.





Model a synchronization problem as possibly non-coprime congruences, derive the consistency condition, and characterize every solution.
Derive why a linear sieve visits each composite exactly once and use the invariant to justify the recurrences for \(\varphi\) and \(\mu\).
Compute \(\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\) for all \(n\le N\) in two ways and compare.
Given a length-\(k\) linear recurrence, derive both its companion-matrix and characteristic-polynomial representations and prove that they agree.
Count strings containing every symbol of a \(k\)-letter alphabet using inclusion–exclusion, then verify by enumeration for small \(n,k\).
For a random walk on a short path with absorbing endpoints, derive the expectation equations and solve them with elimination.

For each exercise, test all small instances. A wrong answer here usually comes from an invariant or ring mistake that will become invisible inside NTT, Min_25, or FPS code.



Use these concise references only for gaps:

CP-Algorithms: extended Euclid (English; use the algebra navigation for modular arithmetic, sieves, and CRT).
AtCoder Library documentation (English contracts for modint, convolution, and floor_sum).
Competitive Programmer’s Handbook, chapters 21–24 (English; compact combinatorics, matrices, probability, and number theory).

Return to the roadmap as soon as the failed diagnostic can be derived and coded from memory. Do not spend weeks re-solving elementary problem sets.

title: 13 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
These problems come last because the main difficulty is classification. Nothing in a World Finals statement announces “use a formal logarithm” or “perform Möbius inversion on this poset.” A capstone attempt should therefore begin without opening the topic tags in this repository. The goal is not to guess a named technique; it is to turn the story into a precise mathematical object until one of the earlier chapters becomes unavoidable.
For example, “sum a function over all pairs” should first become a written sum over \((i,j)\); only then might grouping pairs by \(\gcd(i,j)\) suggest Möbius inversion. “Count drawings up to relabeling” should first name the relabeling group; only then does Burnside give an outer average. This intermediate model is the part worth practising and discussing as a team.


Before coding, write answers to these questions. A good answer is a sentence or equation which could be checked on a three-element example, not a technique name such as “probably NTT.”

What is the mathematical object: residue class, multiplicative function, polynomial/FPS, labelled class, group action, linear operator, random variable, or lattice sum?
Which operation is expensive: pairwise product, convolution, coefficient extraction, repeated transition, divisor sum, or enumeration of symmetric copies?
Which change of basis makes that operation pointwise or triangular?
What is the coefficient ring, and which divisions/roots actually exist?
What brute-force oracle can test the first 20–100 cases?

The ordered set below revisits a few chapter problems in a deliberately tag-free setting and adds one synthesis problem. Treat each as a 3–5 hour team session, not a normal single-person rating drill. Before reading a hint, insist on a proposed invariant: “this table stores …,” “this coefficient counts …,” or “these two configurations are equivalent because ….”




Do not inspect tags, hints, or editorials for the first 90 minutes.
At 90 minutes, compare the three best models you considered. For each, say exactly which object it counts and why it is insufficient or promising. Open only Hint 1 if none gives the target complexity.
At 150 minutes, open Hint 2 and require a written derivation before coding.
At 210 minutes, open Hint 3. Stop after five hours and study the official analysis; continuing an unproductive implementation is not endurance training.
Re-solve from a blank file six weeks later. A remembered code template does not count unless you can re-derive its contract.

Statement · official editorial · English/Japanese
Prerequisites: cyclic multiplicative groups, primitive roots, convolution.
Why here: the hard step is recognizing that a group isomorphism turns a distribution of products into additive convolution.



Hint 1 — recognition

Pairs involving zero contribute zero; after separating them, nonzero residues modulo the fixed prime form a cyclic group.



Hint 2 — reduction

Map each nonzero value to its discrete-log index under a primitive root; multiplication becomes cyclic addition of indices.



Hint 3 — algorithm

Convolve the frequency array and fold indices modulo \(p-1\). Convert each exponent back to its residue, then correct ordered-pair and diagonal contributions to obtain the required unordered-pair sum.





Statement · official analysis · English/Russian
Prerequisites: LCM bounds, linear congruences, generalized CRT.
Why here: a local gcd pattern must first be converted into compatible global row/column congruences, then checked against construction bounds.



Hint 1

Choose a row divisible by every requested entry.



Hint 2

Each desired gcd imposes a congruence on the starting column modulo that entry.



Hint 3

Merge non-coprime congruences, then verify every gcd explicitly; CRT consistency alone is not the full proof.





Statement · official Hello 2019 editorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: divisor zeta/Möbius transforms and arithmetic over \(\mathbb F_2\).
Why here: it combines a non-obvious coordinate system with a representation chosen specifically for a million online operations.



Hint 1

Query parity suggests storing every multiset in a vector space over \(\mathbb F_2\).



Hint 2

Find a transform in which multiset union is addition and the pairwise-GCD product is pointwise multiplication.



Hint 3

Use divisor-incidence vectors packed into bitsets; derive the inverse coefficient needed to recover one exact value.





Statement · GF/FPS derivation · English
Prerequisites: combinatorial decomposition, NTT, FPS inverse and square root.
Why here: the combinatorial equation is short; recognizing and safely computing its algebraic solution is the real test.



Hint 1

Write a generating function for the allowed root weights and decompose a tree at its root.



Hint 2

The two ordered child slots produce a quadratic functional equation.



Hint 3

Select the formal root with the correct constant term and evaluate it using FPS square root and inverse, truncated after every operation.





Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: tree counting, polynomial-valued DP, finite differences or interpolation.
Why here: it requires proving that a huge-domain answer is a low-degree polynomial before any fast evaluation is possible.



Hint 1

Parameterize a subtree by the largest label it may use.



Hint 2

Children multiply; adding the parent takes a prefix sum, so track how the polynomial degree changes.



Hint 3

Compute enough consecutive values and evaluate the resulting bounded-degree polynomial at the large argument.





Statement · official editorial, JA
Prerequisites: Burnside, conjugacy classes of \(S_n\), integer partitions, induced permutation actions, surjective colorings.
Why here: applying Burnside is easy; compressing \(n!\) group elements and counting both vertex-color and edge orbits is the mastery step.



Hint 1

Model an object as a surjective \(K\)-coloring of labelled vertices together with an edge subset, acted on by relabeling vertices.



Hint 2

Group vertex permutations by cycle type rather than enumerating them.



Hint 3

For each vertex cycle type, fixed colorings are constant on vertex cycles and invariant edge sets are constant on pair cycles. Enforce that every color appears before averaging.





Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: ranked subset convolution and AND/OR/XOR transforms.
Why here: the expression must be separated into several distributions, each diagonalized by a different transform, then recombined without losing ordered multiplicities.



Hint 1

Replace indices by a frequency distribution over their bitmask values.



Hint 2

Construct the OR-with-disjointness, singleton, and XOR distributions separately.



Hint 3

Apply the appropriate transform to each stage, include the Fibonacci weights at the right time, and audit whether tuples are ordered.





Statement, ZH · solution index, ZH
Prerequisites: gcd extraction, totient identities, weighted summatory functions, Du Jiao recursion, quotient blocks.
Why here: several familiar identities must be composed before the desired summatory function even becomes visible.



Hint 1

Extract the gcd in the double sum and rewrite the coprime part with a totient identity.



Hint 2

Identify the weighted totient prefix that the quotient blocks require.



Hint 3

Derive a convolution recurrence for that prefix, evaluate polynomial block sums exactly, and remember that the modulus need not justify division.





Finish at least six of the eight, including one of Problems 6–8, under the timed rules. For the remaining problems, a complete postmortem after studying the editorial is preferable to copying an implementation. Then run one five-hour virtual ICPC or Universal Cup contest and classify every unsolved mathematics problem against the course dependency map.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
Symmetry problems ask when two drawings, colorings, or arrangements should be considered the same after an allowed move. They are not “divide by the number of symmetries” problems: one object can be fixed by several moves while another is fixed only by doing nothing. This chapter develops the averaging rule that accounts for that difference.


A finite group \(G\) is a set of allowed moves with an associative composition, an identity move, and an inverse for every move. It acts on a set \(X\) of objects when every \(g\in G\) gives a map \(x\mapsto g\cdot x\), the identity fixes every object, and \(g\cdot(h\cdot x)=(gh)\cdot x\). This last law says that group multiplication and applying moves in sequence use the same convention.
The orbit \(Gx\) is every version of \(x\) reachable by allowed moves. Thus an orbit is one object “up to symmetry.” The stabilizer \(G_x\) is the set of moves leaving \(x\) visually unchanged. They satisfy
\[|Gx|\,|G_x|=|G|. \tag{1}\]
This immediately explains why naive division fails. Under rotation, the three-bead coloring AAA has orbit size \(1\), while AAB has orbit size \(3\). The raw colorings cannot all be assigned weight \(1/3\).
Recognition. First write the actual move set.

necklaces use rotations \(C_n\);
bracelets use rotations and reflections \(D_n\);
a square grid under quarter turns uses a small geometric permutation group;
interchangeable colors introduce another action, usually handled through cycle types or another Burnside layer.

The moves must preserve the problem’s validity condition. If they do not, their orbits are irrelevant to the requested count.



Assume here that both \(G\) and the object set \(X\) are finite. For a move \(g\), let \(\operatorname{Fix}(g)=\{x:g\cdot x=x\}\) be the objects unchanged by that move. Burnside’s lemma says
\[\boxed{|X/G|={1\over|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}(g)|}. \tag{2}\]
It looks surprising because it counts a different quantity for every move. Here is the proof and the meaning. Count pairs \((g,x)\) such that \(gx=x\). Counting by \(g\) gives the numerator. Now look at one orbit \(O\). By (1), each object in \(O\) has \(|G|/|O|\) fixing moves, so the objects of that orbit contribute
\[|O|\cdot {|G|\over|O|}=|G|\]
pairs. Every orbit contributes exactly \(|G|\); dividing by \(|G|\) counts one per orbit.
For a coloring with \(c\) available colors, a move permutes positions into cycles. A fixed coloring must be constant along one cycle, and each cycle independently chooses a color. Thus a move with \(z(g)\) cycles fixes exactly \(c^{z(g)}\) unrestricted colorings.


Rotation by \(r\) on \(n\) positions repeatedly jumps by \(r\). Starting at one position, it returns after \(n/\gcd(n,r)\) jumps, so there are \(\gcd(n,r)\) cycles. Applying (2) gives
\[
N(n,c)={1\over n}\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}c^{\gcd(n,r)}
={1\over n}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(n/d)c^d. \tag{3}
\]
For \(n=3,c=2\), the identity fixes \(2^3=8\) colorings and each nontrivial rotation fixes the two constant colorings. Hence there are \((8+2+2)/3=4\) binary necklaces. The divisor form groups rotations with the same cycle count; it is normally preferable after factoring \(n\).
For bracelets, include reflections too. Derive their cycles from the axis: if \(n\) is odd, each reflection has one fixed position and \((n-1)/2\) pairs. If \(n\) is even, half have two fixed positions and \((n-2)/2\) pairs, while half have no fixed positions and \(n/2\) pairs. This parity split is why a memorized necklace formula does not automatically answer a bracelet task.




Burnside with \(c^{z(g)}\) only counts all colors as freely available. To require, say, exactly three red and two blue beads, attach a marker \(y_i\) to color \(i\). A length-\(j\) cycle painted color \(i\) contributes \(y_i^j\), because that choice uses color \(i\) exactly \(j\) times.
The cycle index records this for every group element:
\[
Z_G(s_1,s_2,\ldots)={1\over|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\prod_{j\ge1}s_j^{c_j(g)}, \tag{4}
\]
where \(c_j(g)\) is the number of length-\(j\) cycles. Substitute
\[s_j\leftarrow y_1^j+\cdots+y_c^j.\]
Then the coefficient of \(y_1^{a_1}\cdots y_c^{a_c}\) is the number of symmetry classes using exactly \(a_i\) positions of color \(i\). For a two-position segment under reflection, the cycle index is
\[\frac12(s_1^2+s_2).\]
After substitution it becomes \(\tfrac12((y_1+y_2)^2+y_1^2+y_2^2)\). The coefficient of \(y_1y_2\) is \(1\): the two raw mixed colorings form one reflection class. The swap itself fixes no mixed coloring, which is why its term is \(y_1^2+y_2^2\) rather than \((y_1+y_2)^2\).
For weighted states with inventory \(A(x)=\sum_w a_wx^w\), where \(a_w\) counts the available states of weight \(w\), use \(s_j\leftarrow A(x^j)\). A cycle of length \(j\) repeats the chosen component \(j\) times, which is exactly why its weight variable becomes \(x^j\). Truncate to the requested total weight throughout.



Burnside is an outer average, not a replacement for the inner combinatorics. For every group element:

find its cycles on the atomic positions;
contract each cycle, because a fixed object must have one state on it;
count valid assignments to those contracted, possibly weighted nodes;
add the result to the Burnside numerator.

For example, a proper coloring fixed by a reflection identifies mirrored vertices. If an edge’s endpoints collapse to one node, that self-loop makes a proper coloring impossible. Other contractions may create parallel edges, which usually do not add a new proper-coloring constraint but may matter for weights. This method cleanly combines symmetry with DP, generating functions, or graph constraints.



For \(S_n\), listing all \(n!\) vertex relabelings is impossible. In problems whose fixed count depends only on cycle lengths, all permutations with the same cycle type behave alike. A type \(1^{m_1}2^{m_2}\cdots\) with \(\sum_i i m_i=n\) has class size
\[\frac{n!}{\prod_i i^{m_i}m_i!}. \tag{5}\]
The denominator has a concrete purpose: rotating a cycle of length \(i\) does not change the cycle, and permuting the \(m_i\) equal-length cycles does not change the permutation. Burnside can therefore sum over integer partitions of \(n\), not over \(n!\) permutations. For each type, construct the induced action on the objects of interest (for unlabeled graphs, on unordered vertex pairs), count its cycles, and multiply by (5). If vertices are colored as well as joined by edges, there are two induced actions: a fixed coloring is constant on each vertex cycle, while a fixed edge set is constant on each unordered-pair cycle. Enforce a requirement such as “every color is used” inside that fixed count, for example by inclusion–exclusion over missing colors.




Division by \(|G|\) modulo prime \(p\) requires \(p\nmid |G|\). Otherwise divide exactly before reduction, or use a problem-specific integral rearrangement.
A reflection and a rotation with the same order need not have the same cycles.
If colors are themselves indistinguishable, ordinary position Burnside still treats color names as distinct; model the color symmetry too.
Exact multiplicities require coefficient extraction from (4), not simply colors ^ cycles.
On a two- or three-position toy case, enumerate raw objects, group their orbits by hand, and compare with the Burnside numerator before coding.

title: 14 — Modular Combinatorics and q-Analogues
text:
This chapter begins where the familiar formula
\[\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\]
stops being a legal modular computation. A factorial table modulo a prime \(p\) only supports division while every denominator is nonzero, hence while the relevant factorial arguments are below \(p\). The two warning signs are \(n\ge p\) and a composite modulus. The cure is to separate the powers of each prime (which are not invertible) from the remaining unit part (which is).
The notation \(v_p(x)\) means “the exponent of \(p\) in \(x\)”; for example, \(v_2(40)=3\). It is the bookkeeper that tells us exactly when a binomial coefficient becomes zero modulo a prime power.


For prime \(p\), write \(n=\sum n_i p^{i}\) and \(k=\sum k_i p^{i}\), where each digit is in \([0,p)\). Lucas gives
\[\binom nk\equiv\prod_i\binom{n_i}{k_i}\pmod p.\]
So one huge binomial coefficient becomes a product of tiny digit-level ones. For example, \(5=(101)_2\) and \(2=(010)_2\), so Lucas includes \(\binom 0 1=0\) and therefore \(\binom52\equiv0\pmod2\).
Kummer says \(v_p\binom nk\) is the number of carries in base \(p\) when adding \(k\) and \(n-k\). It supplies more information than the yes/no answer modulo \(p\): a carry count of \(c\) says the coefficient is divisible by \(p^c\). In the example above, \(2+(5-2)=(10)_2+(11)_2=(101)_2\) has one carry, agreeing with \(v_2\binom52=1\). A digit with \(k_i>n_i\) is exactly a borrow when subtracting \(k\) from \(n\), equivalently a carry in that addition. Lucas is the value theorem; Kummer is the divisibility theorem.



For \(q=p^{e}\), first use Legendre’s formula
\[v_p(n!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac n{p^j}\right\rfloor.\]
Then represent a factorial as \(n!=p^vU(n)\), where \(U(n)\) is not divisible by \(p\) and is therefore invertible modulo \(p^e\). Compute this p-free factorial by multiplying only terms not divisible by \(p\) in complete blocks, then recursing on \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\): the recursive call accounts for the factors left after removing one \(p\) from every multiple of \(p\). This is the reason a prime-power factorial routine is more than a factorial table. Then
\[\binom nk=p^{v_p(n!)-v_p(k!)-v_p((n-k)!)}
U(n)U(k)^{-1}U(n-k)^{-1}\pmod {p^e}.\]
If the exponent is at least \(e\), the answer is zero modulo \(p^e\). Otherwise all inverted parts are units and the displayed expression is valid. For a composite modulus \(m\), factor \(m\) into coprime prime powers, solve one local problem per factor, and use CRT to select the unique residue modulo \(m\) with those local residues. Never cancel numerator and denominator directly in \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\): a nonzero residue can still be a non-unit, such as \(2\) modulo \(6\).



Here \(q\) has a different role from the modulus above: it is either a formal variable or the size of a finite field. When \(q\) is a prime power, the Gaussian (or q-) binomial coefficient counts \(r\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_q^{n}\):
\[\binom nr_q=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{q^{n-i}-1}{q^{r-i}-1}.\]
To see the product, count ordered independent vectors in two ways. The first vector has \(q^n-1\) choices, the next has \(q^n-q\) choices, and so on; divide by the number \((q^r-1)(q^r-q)\cdots(q^r-q^{r-1})\) of ordered bases of one fixed \(r\)-subspace. The same polynomial is the inversion generating polynomial for binary strings with \(r\) ones, and the area generating polynomial for partitions inside an \(r\times(n-r)\) rectangle. Thus \(\binom42_q=
1+q+2q^2+q^3+q^4\) records how many such objects have each statistic value.
The recurrence
\[\binom nr_q=\binom{n-1}r_q+q^{n-r}\binom{n-1}{r-1}_q\]
remains valid even when the product formula appears to divide by zero. Fix a hyperplane \(H\cong\mathbb F_q^{n-1}\). An \(r\)-subspace is either contained in \(H\), giving the first term, or meets \(H\) in an \((r-1)\)-subspace; the latter case has \(q^{n-r}\) extensions, giving the second term. It is often the safest way to compute a whole table. For a fixed numerical \(q\) modulo a prime \(P\), precompute q-integers and q-factorials only while their factors are invertible. If some \(q^i-1\) vanishes modulo \(P\), ordinary division is invalid even though the Gaussian binomial itself remains defined. Use the division-free recurrence, a proved q-Lucas theorem when its hypotheses match, or cancel cyclotomic-factor exponents before evaluation.



Factorial-scaled EGF formulas require \(1,\ldots,N\) to be invertible. When \(N\ge p\), use base-\(p\) digit structure, recurrences that avoid division, or algorithms specifically designed for small characteristic. This affects Stirling rows, Bell numbers, FPS integration, and q-factorials—not just \({n\choose k}\).




Prime modulus and \(n<p\): factorial tables.
Small prime and huge \(n\): Lucas; use Kummer to reason about zeros.
Prime power: valuation plus unit factorial.
General composite modulus: prime powers plus generalized CRT.
q-analogue: identify whether it counts subspaces, inversions, or partitions.

Before coding, write down the modulus factorization, the largest factorial argument, and every quantity you intend to invert. Those three lines usually choose the method and expose an invalid factorial-table solution immediately.

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text:
A polynomial is a finite coefficient array, but it is useful to think of it as a compact description of size-indexed choices: \([x^k]A(x)\) is the answer for total size \(k\). This chapter explains why the fast operations work and when their algebraic preconditions hold. It assumes your library already supplies tested convolution and basic polynomial operations.


For \(C(x)=A(x)B(x)\),
\[c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j. \tag{1}\]
Each summand chooses an \(i\)-sized object from \(A\) and a \((k-i)\)-sized object from \(B\). This “split a total” meaning is why convolution occurs in counting, DP merging, and formal power series.
The transform idea is simple: evaluate polynomials at a specially chosen set of points. At every point \(z\), \((AB)(z)=A(z)B(z)\), so multiplication becomes pointwise. An FFT uses complex roots of unity; an NTT uses roots of unity in a finite field. Interpolation returns to coefficient form.


For an NTT of length \(L=2^s\) modulo prime \(p\), we need \(L\mid p-1\) so the field has a primitive \(L\)th root of unity. The result length must cover every possible degree, so \(L\ge |A|+|B|-1\). For example, \(998244353=119\cdot2^{23}+1\) supports powers of two through \(2^{23}\).
If the answer is modulo an arbitrary \(m\), do not pretend one NTT prime computes it. Convolve under one or more NTT-friendly primes, reconstruct the integer coefficient by CRT (or use Garner to perform the same reconstruction directly modulo \(m\) when the bounded coefficients are nonnegative), then reduce. Garner avoids storing a huge reconstructed integer; it does not remove the reconstruction-range requirement. For signed coefficients, centered CRT must also determine whether the representative means \(c\) or \(c-P\), where \(P\) is the product of auxiliary primes; a direct Garner residue needs the corresponding sign correction modulo \(m\). The number of primes is determined by a proved bound on the integer coefficients: for a signed coefficient of absolute value at most \(B\), centered CRT needs a product of moduli greater than \(2B\). Three primes are a convention, not a proof. Complex FFT instead needs coefficient splitting and a rounding-error bound.




Given \(A=BQ+R\) with \(\deg R<\deg B\), ordinary long division removes the highest remaining term one at a time. Reversal makes those highest terms become the low-degree terms of a formal power series, where inversion is fast. If \(\deg A<\deg B\), there is nothing to divide: return \(Q=0,R=A\).
Let \(k=\deg A-\deg B+1\). Define \(\operatorname{rev}_k(F)\) by reading from \(F\)’s actual leading coefficient downward, retaining \(k\) coefficients and padding with zeros only after its constant term. Then
\[
\operatorname{rev}_k(Q)
\equiv \operatorname{rev}_k(A)\operatorname{rev}_k(B)^{-1}\pmod{x^k}. \tag{2}
\]
Why is this legal? The leading coefficient of \(B\) becomes the constant coefficient of \(\operatorname{rev}_k(B)\); it can be inverted precisely when the leading coefficient is a unit (equivalently nonzero over a field). Terms from \(R\) land beyond the first \(k\) reversed coefficients and disappear modulo \(x^k\). Reverse the quotient back, then compute \(R=A-BQ\).
This costs \(O(M(n))\) with fast multiplication. Over a general ring it requires the leading coefficient of \(B\) to be a unit. In particular, modulo a composite number a nonzero leading coefficient might not be invertible, so this division contract can fail.



To evaluate \(f\) at points \(x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}\), build a balanced tree. A leaf stores \(x-x_i\); an internal node stores the product of its children:
\[P_v(x)=\prod_{i\text{ below }v}(x-x_i).\]
At the root, replace \(f\) by its remainder modulo \(P_{root}\). A polynomial remainder modulo \(x-x_i\) is its value at \(x_i\), so recursively passing the remainder modulo each child reaches \(f(x_i)\) at every leaf. This is the same divide-and-conquer idea as a segment tree: a node stores the polynomial that vanishes at all points in its interval.
If \(\deg f=O(m)\), fast division at each level costs \(O(M(m)\log m)\) in the balanced case. For a higher-degree \(f\), first reducing it modulo \(P_{root}\) adds the cost of that division. For a small number of points, Horner’s rule is simpler and often faster; use a product tree only when the asymptotic saving matters.



Now suppose the points \(x_i\) are pairwise distinct in the coefficient field and the desired values \(y_i\) are known. Let
\[P(x)=\prod_i(x-x_i).\]
The polynomial \(P(x)/(x-x_i)\) vanishes at every \(x_j\) except \(x_i\). Dividing it by its value there, \(P'(x_i)\), creates a basis polynomial that is \(1\) at \(x_i\) and \(0\) at every other sample. Therefore
\[f(x)=\sum_i y_i\frac{P(x)}{(x-x_i)P'(x_i)}. \tag{3}\]
This formula is not magic: each summand is responsible for exactly one sample. Evaluate \(P'\) at all points via the product tree, place \(w_i=y_i/P'(x_i)\) at leaves, and merge children as
\[F_v=F_LP_R+F_RP_L.\]
At the root this is (3), in \(O(M(n)\log n)\). If points repeat, \(P'(x_i)=0\) and ordinary interpolation is undefined; repeated-value data needs the stronger Hermite-interpolation problem.
For values at the \(n+1\) consecutive points \(0,\ldots,n\), the denominators simplify to \(i!(-1)^{n-i}(n-i)!\). Prefix and suffix products of \((t-j)\) evaluate (3) at one arbitrary \(t\) in \(O(n)\). Factorials must be invertible, so normally \(n<MOD\).



We want the coefficients of \(f(x+c)\), not just its value at one point. Expanding each monomial gives
\[[x^k]f(x+c)=\sum_{i\ge k}a_i\binom ikc^{i-k}. \tag{4}\]
This says degree \(i\) contributes to every lower degree \(k\). Expand the binomial coefficient and reverse the \(a_i i!\) array; (4) becomes one convolution with the array \(c^j/j!\), followed by division by \(k!\). If \(n=\deg f\), put \(u_{n-i}=a_i i!\) and \(v_j=c^j/j!\). Then
\[\frac{(u*v)_{n-k}}{k!}=
\sum_{i\ge k}a_i\binom ikc^{i-k},\]
so \((u*v)_{n-k}\) is \(k!\) times the shifted coefficient of \(x^k\); the final division by \(k!\) is essential. For example, if \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(c=1\), then the convolution entries at indices \(2,1,0\) are \(1,2,2\), and division by \(0!,1!,2!\) gives the coefficients \(1,2,1\) of \((x+1)^2\). The reversal lines up \(i-k\) as a convolution index. As with binomial transforms, this needs the factorials through the working degree to be units; it is normally used over a prime modulus larger than that degree.



For \(\prod_i A_i(x)\), multiplying factors one after another repeatedly makes a large polynomial absorb a tiny one. A divide-and-conquer product tree, or a priority queue that merges the two smallest degrees, keeps products balanced. For total output degree \(N\), this is typically \(O(M(N)\log k)\).
If the question only asks through degree \(D\), truncate after each merge. In a knapsack-style product such as \(\prod_i(1+x^{w_i})\), coefficients above \(D\) can never influence lower coefficients later, so retaining them only wastes time and memory.




Before an NTT, verify both the required length and the root-of-unity condition.
Before a polynomial inverse, verify a nonzero/invertible constant term; before division, verify the leading coefficient condition instead.
Normalize negative coefficients in the target ring.
For CRT convolution, prove the reconstruction range covers a coefficient.
Interpolation requires distinct sample points; consecutive-point formulas additionally need nonzero factorial denominators.
Check a small product, quotient/remainder identity, and interpolation samples independently of the fast routine.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Ordinary sieves compute every value through \(N\); summatory sieves compute only
\[F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\]
when \(N\) is too large to visit. Here “compute only” does not mean magically skip information: it means find a recurrence whose arguments repeat among a small set of floor quotients. The art is choosing the correct structure:

Du Jiao sieve: an easy Dirichlet convolution isolates \(F(N)\).
Min_25 sieve: \(f\) is multiplicative and \(f(p)\) is a low-degree polynomial in \(p\).
Powerful-number sieve: remove an easy function agreeing with \(f\) on primes, leaving support only on numbers whose prime exponents are never one.

Before this chapter, master multiplicative functions, Möbius inversion, and quotient grouping in Chapter 02.


Every recursive call in these methods should normally be one of the distinct values \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\). This is a small state space because values below \(\sqrt N\) can occur directly, while every value above it equals \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\) for some \(i<\sqrt N\). There are fewer than \(2\sqrt N\) values in total. Two common indexing schemes are:

store large values in a hash map and precompute all values up to a cutoff;
map \(v\) to \(v\) itself if \(v≤\sqrt{N}\), otherwise to \(N/v\) in a second array.

For \(N=20\), the distinct states are \(20,10,6,5,4,3,2,1\), rather than twenty different arguments. This is the object being memoized; quotient grouping is what makes a recurrence over all divisors practical.
Never accidentally memoize arbitrary arguments: that can turn an intended \(O(\sqrt{N})\) state set into linear space.



Suppose \(h=f*g\) and the prefixes of \(h\) and \(g\) are cheap. We want \(F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\). Start by summing the definition of convolution:
\[H(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\sum_{d\mid n}f(n/d)g(d).\]
Writing \(n=dk\) makes the meaning visible: for each possible \(d\), the allowed \(k\) run through \(1,\ldots,\lfloor N/d\rfloor\). Swapping those two sums gives
\[H(N)=\sum_{d\le N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If \(g(1)=1\), the \(d=1\) term is exactly \(F(N)\); move every other term to the other side:
\[F(N)=H(N)-\sum_{d=2}^{N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If instead \(g(1)\) is another unit, divide the whole equation by \(g(1)\) after isolating \(g(1)F(N)\); without an invertible \(g(1)\) this recurrence is not an algorithmic contract. Commutativity lets you swap the names of \(f,g\) if the other factor has easier prefix sums. The remaining formula appears to have \(N\) terms, but all indices \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\) repeat. Group a block \(l\le d\le r\) with one quotient \(q\); its total coefficient is \(G(r)-G(l-1)\). That quotient grouping is the speedup, not the recurrence alone.


Let \(M(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu(n)\). The identity \(\mu*1=\varepsilon\) says that the convolution prefix \(H(N)\) is \(1\) for every \(N\ge1\). Here \(g=1\), so a block of indices \([l,r]\) has coefficient \(r-l+1\). Substitution gives
\[
M(N)=1-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)M(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\qquad r_N(l)=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{\lfloor N/l\rfloor}\right\rfloor.
\]
Here \(\mathcal B_N\) is the set of quotient-block starts: begin with \(l=2\) and repeatedly replace \(l\) by \(r_N(l)+1\). It is not the set of every integer from \(2\) through \(N\).
Let \(\Phi(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\varphi(n)\). The identity \(\varphi*1=\operatorname{id}\) says its convolution prefix is \(1+2+\cdots+N=T(N)=N(N+1)/2\), giving
\[
\Phi(N)=T(N)-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)\Phi(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\]
with the same definitions of \(\mathcal B_N\) and \(r_N(l)\).
Precompute both functions to \(B\) by linear sieve and memoize only larger quotient states. A cutoff around \(N^{2/3}\) gives the classic practical complexity near \(O(N^{2/3})\), though tuning and the query model affect constants.
The quadratic scale of \(\sum\varphi(n)\) requires wide intermediates. Reduce modulo the problem modulus inside every operation if that is what the statement asks.




Name the wanted prefix \(F\).
Find \(g\) so \(h=f*g\) has an elementary prefix.
Sum \(h(n)\) for \(n≤N\), swap \(n=dk\), and isolate \(F(N)\).
Express coefficient sums on \([l,r]\) with prefix formulas.
Confirm every recursive argument is \(\lfloor N/l\rfloor\) and smaller than \(N\).





Min_25 first solves a narrower problem: quickly find sums over primes, such as \(\sum_{p\le w}p^k\), at every quotient state \(w=\lfloor N/l\rfloor\). Initialize
\[g_k(w)=\sum_{i=2}^{w}i^{k}.\]
At the start, \(g_k(w)\) is the sum over all integers \(2,\ldots,w\). Process primes \(p\) in increasing order. At the \(p\) stage, subtract the composites whose smallest prime factor is \(p\); for every state \(w\ge p^2\) this is
\[g_k(w)\mathrel{-}=p^{k}\left(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)-S_k(p-1)\right),\]
where \(S_k(p-1)=\sum_{q<p,q prime}q^{k}\). After processing all \(p≤\sqrt{N}\), \(g_k(w)=\sum_{q≤w,q prime}q^{k}\).
Why \(p^2\)? Any composite first removed at this stage has least prime factor \(p\), hence it is \(p\cdot x\) with \(x\ge p\). Just before the \(p\) stage, \(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)\) consists of two kinds of surviving entries: primes below \(p\), which are deliberately retained as final prime answers, and integers having no prime factor below \(p\). Only the second kind can be a valid cofactor \(x\), so \(S_k(p-1)\) removes the retained small primes. Updating states in descending order prevents the right side from using values already modified by the current prime. After all relevant stages, only prime contributions remain.
For \(k=0\), this computes \(\pi(w)\). Its practical complexity for one \(N\) is about \(O(N^{3/4}/\log N)\) time and \(O(\sqrt{N})\) memory.



Min_25 extends that prime-sum engine to a multiplicative function. Assume \(f\) is multiplicative, each \(f(p^{e})\) is computable in \(O(1)\), and the prime values, not necessarily all prime-power values, satisfy
\[f(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}c_kp^{k}\]
for small fixed \(K\). Run the prime-sum sieve for each required power \(k\); combine the arrays to obtain
\[G_f(x)=\sum_{p\le x}f(p).\]
The prime-sum sieve gives the contribution of prime numbers. To cover every composite exactly once, enumerate it by its least prime and the exact exponent of that prime. Index primes from \(p_0=2\) and set \(G_f(p_{-1})=0\). Define \(S(x,y)\) as the sum of \(f(n)\) for \(2\le n\le x\) whose least prime is at least \(p_y\). Calls maintain \(p_{y-1}\le x\) (with the \(y=0\) sentinel understood), so its prime-only base contribution is \(G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})\) and is zero when the interval contains no prime. For every possible least prime \(p_i\), enumerate an exponent \(e\ge1\). The term with \(S\) counts numbers \(p_i^e m\) where \(m>1\) has no prime factor at most \(p_i\); the separate term counts pure powers (the prime \(p_i\) itself is already in the base term):
\[
S(x,y)=G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})+
\sum_{\substack{i\ge y\\p_i^2\le x}}
\sum_{\substack{e\ge1\\p_i^{e+1}\le x}}
\left(f(p_i^e)S(\lfloor x/p_i^e\rfloor,i+1)+f(p_i^{e+1})\right).
\]
Finally \(f(1)+S(N,0)=1+S(N,0)\) is the prefix, using the standard convention for a multiplicative function. The shift in the pure-power exponent is deliberate: as \(e=1,2,\ldots\), those terms list \(p_i^2,p_i^3,\ldots\) exactly once, while the cofactor term uses \(p_i^e\) as the exact valuation. The condition \(p_i^{e+1}\le x\) also safely ends the cofactor branch: any permitted nontrivial cofactor is at least \(p_{i+1}>p_i\). This decomposition is unique.
As a hand check, take \(f(n)=1\) and \(x=10\). The base term counts the four primes \(2,3,5,7\). The branch for least prime \(2\) contributes \(6,10\) from \(2\cdot\{3,5\}\) and the pure powers \(4,8\); the branch for least prime \(3\) contributes the pure power \(9\). Together with \(f(1)\) these are all ten integers, each assigned to exactly one least-prime branch.
Typical complexity is \(O(K N^{3/4}/\log N)\) for the prime sums plus roughly \(O(N^{3/4}/\log N)\) enumeration, with \(O((K+1)\sqrt{N})\) storage. Exact bounds and constants depend on the implementation and \(f\).
Applicability signals. \(N\) is around \(10^{9}–10^{12}\), the statement gives a multiplicative function through its prime powers, and its value at a prime is polynomial (examples: \(\varphi(p)=p-1\), \(\mu(p)=-1\), \(\sigma_k(p)=1+p^{k}\)).
Non-applicable cases. If \(f(p)\) depends on an arbitrary property of \(p\) for which no fast prime prefix exists, standard Min_25 has no base data. If only \(\mu/\varphi\) prefixes are needed, Du Jiao is simpler.



A positive integer is powerful if every prime dividing it has exponent at least two. For example, \(72=2^3\cdot3^2\) is powerful whereas \(12=2^2\cdot3\) is not. The count through \(N\) is \(O(\sqrt N)\) because every powerful integer has the unique representation
\[n=a^2b^3,\qquad b\text{ square-free}.\]
For each prime exponent \(e\ge2\), choose the unique \(e=2u+3v\) with \(v\in\{0,1\}\); the primes with \(v=1\) form \(b\). Consequently \(b\le N^{1/3}\) and \(a\le\sqrt{N/b^3}\). Summing over \(b\) gives \(\sqrt N\sum_b b^{-3/2}=O(\sqrt N)\) candidates. The requirement that \(b\) be square-free is what makes the representation unique.
This sparsity yields another generic strategy. Choose an easy multiplicative \(g\) agreeing with \(f\) on primes, and define
\[h=f*g^{-1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=h*g.\]
Because multiplicative functions have value \(1\) at \(1\), the prime-power convolution identity gives \(h(p)=f(p)-g(p)=0\). Multiplicativity then forces \(h(n)=0\) whenever any prime has exponent exactly one: its product over prime-power factors contains \(h(p)=0\). Thus \(h\) is supported on powerful numbers. Let \(G(x)=\sum_{n\le x}g(n)\). In the convolution \(f=h*g\), choosing a divisor \(d\) for the \(h\) factor leaves a \(g\) factor through \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\); summing those choices gives
\[F(N)=\sum_{d\le N\atop d\text{ powerful}}h(d)G(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
Compute local prime-power coefficients from
\[f(p^{e})=\sum_{j=0}^{e}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}),\]
so \(h(1)=1\), \(h(p)=0\), and for \(e≥2\),
\[h(p^{e})=f(p^{e})-\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}).\]
Enumerate powerful numbers by DFS over increasing primes, choosing exponent zero or at least two; accumulate \(h(d)G(N/d)\). Prune when \(d·p²>N\). Alternatively enumerate the unique \(a²b³\) representation when the coefficient is easier to recover that way.
This method is attractive when \(G(x)\) is elementary or already available and \(h(p^{e})\) is cheap. Complexity is commonly around \(O(\sqrt{N} \operatorname{polylog} N)\) plus the cost of obtaining \(G\) and primes, but must be derived for the exact enumeration.


To count integers \(n>1\) representable as \(a^{b}\) with \(a,b>1\), enumerate exponents but remove duplicate representations. If \(n=\prod_i p_i^{e_i}\), its maximal possible exponent is \(\gcd_i e_i\); thus \(n\) is a nontrivial perfect power exactly when this gcd exceeds one. Möbius inversion over exponents, or counting by the maximal exponent, avoids double counting. Integer kth roots must be corrected with exact 128-bit power comparisons—floating- point pow alone is unsafe near \(10^{18}\).

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Every recursive call in these methods should normally be one of the distinct values \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\). This is a small state space because values below \(\sqrt N\) can occur directly, while every value above it equals \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\) for some \(i<\sqrt N\). There are fewer than \(2\sqrt N\) values in total. Two common indexing schemes are:

store large values in a hash map and precompute all values up to a cutoff;
map \(v\) to \(v\) itself if \(v≤\sqrt{N}\), otherwise to \(N/v\) in a second array.

For \(N=20\), the distinct states are \(20,10,6,5,4,3,2,1\), rather than twenty different arguments. This is the object being memoized; quotient grouping is what makes a recurrence over all divisors practical.
Never accidentally memoize arbitrary arguments: that can turn an intended \(O(\sqrt{N})\) state set into linear space.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Suppose \(h=f*g\) and the prefixes of \(h\) and \(g\) are cheap. We want \(F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\). Start by summing the definition of convolution:
\[H(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\sum_{d\mid n}f(n/d)g(d).\]
Writing \(n=dk\) makes the meaning visible: for each possible \(d\), the allowed \(k\) run through \(1,\ldots,\lfloor N/d\rfloor\). Swapping those two sums gives
\[H(N)=\sum_{d\le N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If \(g(1)=1\), the \(d=1\) term is exactly \(F(N)\); move every other term to the other side:
\[F(N)=H(N)-\sum_{d=2}^{N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If instead \(g(1)\) is another unit, divide the whole equation by \(g(1)\) after isolating \(g(1)F(N)\); without an invertible \(g(1)\) this recurrence is not an algorithmic contract. Commutativity lets you swap the names of \(f,g\) if the other factor has easier prefix sums. The remaining formula appears to have \(N\) terms, but all indices \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\) repeat. Group a block \(l\le d\le r\) with one quotient \(q\); its total coefficient is \(G(r)-G(l-1)\). That quotient grouping is the speedup, not the recurrence alone.


Let \(M(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu(n)\). The identity \(\mu*1=\varepsilon\) says that the convolution prefix \(H(N)\) is \(1\) for every \(N\ge1\). Here \(g=1\), so a block of indices \([l,r]\) has coefficient \(r-l+1\). Substitution gives
\[
M(N)=1-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)M(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\qquad r_N(l)=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{\lfloor N/l\rfloor}\right\rfloor.
\]
Here \(\mathcal B_N\) is the set of quotient-block starts: begin with \(l=2\) and repeatedly replace \(l\) by \(r_N(l)+1\). It is not the set of every integer from \(2\) through \(N\).
Let \(\Phi(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\varphi(n)\). The identity \(\varphi*1=\operatorname{id}\) says its convolution prefix is \(1+2+\cdots+N=T(N)=N(N+1)/2\), giving
\[
\Phi(N)=T(N)-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)\Phi(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\]
with the same definitions of \(\mathcal B_N\) and \(r_N(l)\).
Precompute both functions to \(B\) by linear sieve and memoize only larger quotient states. A cutoff around \(N^{2/3}\) gives the classic practical complexity near \(O(N^{2/3})\), though tuning and the query model affect constants.
The quadratic scale of \(\sum\varphi(n)\) requires wide intermediates. Reduce modulo the problem modulus inside every operation if that is what the statement asks.




Name the wanted prefix \(F\).
Find \(g\) so \(h=f*g\) has an elementary prefix.
Sum \(h(n)\) for \(n≤N\), swap \(n=dk\), and isolate \(F(N)\).
