title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Min_25 first solves a narrower problem: quickly find sums over primes, such as \(\sum_{p\le w}p^k\), at every quotient state \(w=\lfloor N/l\rfloor\). Initialize
\[g_k(w)=\sum_{i=2}^{w}i^{k}.\]
At the start, \(g_k(w)\) is the sum over all integers \(2,\ldots,w\). Process primes \(p\) in increasing order. At the \(p\) stage, subtract the composites whose smallest prime factor is \(p\); for every state \(w\ge p^2\) this is
\[g_k(w)\mathrel{-}=p^{k}\left(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)-S_k(p-1)\right),\]
where \(S_k(p-1)=\sum_{q<p,q prime}q^{k}\). After processing all \(p≤\sqrt{N}\), \(g_k(w)=\sum_{q≤w,q prime}q^{k}\).
Why \(p^2\)? Any composite first removed at this stage has least prime factor \(p\), hence it is \(p\cdot x\) with \(x\ge p\). Just before the \(p\) stage, \(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)\) consists of two kinds of surviving entries: primes below \(p\), which are deliberately retained as final prime answers, and integers having no prime factor below \(p\). Only the second kind can be a valid cofactor \(x\), so \(S_k(p-1)\) removes the retained small primes. Updating states in descending order prevents the right side from using values already modified by the current prime. After all relevant stages, only prime contributions remain.
For \(k=0\), this computes \(\pi(w)\). Its practical complexity for one \(N\) is about \(O(N^{3/4}/\log N)\) time and \(O(\sqrt{N})\) memory.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Min_25 extends that prime-sum engine to a multiplicative function. Assume \(f\) is multiplicative, each \(f(p^{e})\) is computable in \(O(1)\), and the prime values, not necessarily all prime-power values, satisfy
\[f(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}c_kp^{k}\]
for small fixed \(K\). Run the prime-sum sieve for each required power \(k\); combine the arrays to obtain
\[G_f(x)=\sum_{p\le x}f(p).\]
The prime-sum sieve gives the contribution of prime numbers. To cover every composite exactly once, enumerate it by its least prime and the exact exponent of that prime. Index primes from \(p_0=2\) and set \(G_f(p_{-1})=0\). Define \(S(x,y)\) as the sum of \(f(n)\) for \(2\le n\le x\) whose least prime is at least \(p_y\). Calls maintain \(p_{y-1}\le x\) (with the \(y=0\) sentinel understood), so its prime-only base contribution is \(G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})\) and is zero when the interval contains no prime. For every possible least prime \(p_i\), enumerate an exponent \(e\ge1\). The term with \(S\) counts numbers \(p_i^e m\) where \(m>1\) has no prime factor at most \(p_i\); the separate term counts pure powers (the prime \(p_i\) itself is already in the base term):
\[
S(x,y)=G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})+
\sum_{\substack{i\ge y\\p_i^2\le x}}
\sum_{\substack{e\ge1\\p_i^{e+1}\le x}}
\left(f(p_i^e)S(\lfloor x/p_i^e\rfloor,i+1)+f(p_i^{e+1})\right).
\]
Finally \(f(1)+S(N,0)=1+S(N,0)\) is the prefix, using the standard convention for a multiplicative function. The shift in the pure-power exponent is deliberate: as \(e=1,2,\ldots\), those terms list \(p_i^2,p_i^3,\ldots\) exactly once, while the cofactor term uses \(p_i^e\) as the exact valuation. The condition \(p_i^{e+1}\le x\) also safely ends the cofactor branch: any permitted nontrivial cofactor is at least \(p_{i+1}>p_i\). This decomposition is unique.
As a hand check, take \(f(n)=1\) and \(x=10\). The base term counts the four primes \(2,3,5,7\). The branch for least prime \(2\) contributes \(6,10\) from \(2\cdot\{3,5\}\) and the pure powers \(4,8\); the branch for least prime \(3\) contributes the pure power \(9\). Together with \(f(1)\) these are all ten integers, each assigned to exactly one least-prime branch.
Typical complexity is \(O(K N^{3/4}/\log N)\) for the prime sums plus roughly \(O(N^{3/4}/\log N)\) enumeration, with \(O((K+1)\sqrt{N})\) storage. Exact bounds and constants depend on the implementation and \(f\).
Applicability signals. \(N\) is around \(10^{9}–10^{12}\), the statement gives a multiplicative function through its prime powers, and its value at a prime is polynomial (examples: \(\varphi(p)=p-1\), \(\mu(p)=-1\), \(\sigma_k(p)=1+p^{k}\)).
Non-applicable cases. If \(f(p)\) depends on an arbitrary property of \(p\) for which no fast prime prefix exists, standard Min_25 has no base data. If only \(\mu/\varphi\) prefixes are needed, Du Jiao is simpler.

title: 03 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
A positive integer is powerful if every prime dividing it has exponent at least two. For example, \(72=2^3\cdot3^2\) is powerful whereas \(12=2^2\cdot3\) is not. The count through \(N\) is \(O(\sqrt N)\) because every powerful integer has the unique representation
\[n=a^2b^3,\qquad b\text{ square-free}.\]
For each prime exponent \(e\ge2\), choose the unique \(e=2u+3v\) with \(v\in\{0,1\}\); the primes with \(v=1\) form \(b\). Consequently \(b\le N^{1/3}\) and \(a\le\sqrt{N/b^3}\). Summing over \(b\) gives \(\sqrt N\sum_b b^{-3/2}=O(\sqrt N)\) candidates. The requirement that \(b\) be square-free is what makes the representation unique.
This sparsity yields another generic strategy. Choose an easy multiplicative \(g\) agreeing with \(f\) on primes, and define
\[h=f*g^{-1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=h*g.\]
Because multiplicative functions have value \(1\) at \(1\), the prime-power convolution identity gives \(h(p)=f(p)-g(p)=0\). Multiplicativity then forces \(h(n)=0\) whenever any prime has exponent exactly one: its product over prime-power factors contains \(h(p)=0\). Thus \(h\) is supported on powerful numbers. Let \(G(x)=\sum_{n\le x}g(n)\). In the convolution \(f=h*g\), choosing a divisor \(d\) for the \(h\) factor leaves a \(g\) factor through \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\); summing those choices gives
\[F(N)=\sum_{d\le N\atop d\text{ powerful}}h(d)G(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
Compute local prime-power coefficients from
\[f(p^{e})=\sum_{j=0}^{e}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}),\]
so \(h(1)=1\), \(h(p)=0\), and for \(e≥2\),
\[h(p^{e})=f(p^{e})-\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}).\]
Enumerate powerful numbers by DFS over increasing primes, choosing exponent zero or at least two; accumulate \(h(d)G(N/d)\). Prune when \(d·p²>N\). Alternatively enumerate the unique \(a²b³\) representation when the coefficient is easier to recover that way.
This method is attractive when \(G(x)\) is elementary or already available and \(h(p^{e})\) is cheap. Complexity is commonly around \(O(\sqrt{N} \operatorname{polylog} N)\) plus the cost of obtaining \(G\) and primes, but must be derived for the exact enumeration.


To count integers \(n>1\) representable as \(a^{b}\) with \(a,b>1\), enumerate exponents but remove duplicate representations. If \(n=\prod_i p_i^{e_i}\), its maximal possible exponent is \(\gcd_i e_i\); thus \(n\) is a nontrivial perfect power exactly when this gcd exceeds one. Möbius inversion over exponents, or counting by the maximal exponent, avoids double counting. Integer kth roots must be corrected with exact 128-bit power comparisons—floating- point pow alone is unsafe near \(10^{18}\).

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
Linear algebra appears whenever constraints are linear, path choices form an XOR space, spanning trees must be counted, or a long recurrence must be compressed. The common idea is to replace many objects by coordinates in a vector space and then use reversible row operations. Always identify the scalar domain first: real numbers, \(\mathbb F_p\), and \(\mathbb F_2\) have different numerical and structural hazards.


Over a field, row operations preserve the solution set because they merely replace one equation by an equivalent linear combination of equations. Maintain a pivot row; for each column choose a nonzero entry, swap it to that row, normalize, and eliminate. A pivot in the coefficient matrix records one independent equation, so \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) is the number of such pivots. For a system with \(r\) equations and \(c\) unknowns, a zero row with a nonzero augmented entry means inconsistency; otherwise the augmented matrix has the same rank as \(A\) and there are \(c-\operatorname{rank}(A)\) free variables. Over \(\mathbb F_q\), that means exactly \(q^{\,c-\operatorname{rank}(A)}\) solutions; over an infinite field it describes a solution affine space of that dimension.
For example, over \(\mathbb F_5\), \(x+y=1\), \(2x+3y=0\) becomes \(y=3,x=3\) after subtracting twice the first row. The integer solution is irrelevant: the field is part of the question. Dense elimination costs \(O(rc\min(r,c))\). For determinant, do not normalize: each row swap negates the answer, multiply by the pivot, then eliminate below using the current entry divided by the pivot. Composite moduli are not fields: a nonzero pivot may be noninvertible. Use prime-factor methods, fraction-free elimination, or exact integer algorithms instead.



A set of machine words is a vector set whose coordinates are bits, with XOR as vector addition. Keep at most one pivot per highest bit. Inserting a word means XORing away known highest bits; if nothing remains it was already a linear combination of earlier words, otherwise it adds one independent direction.
Insertion costs \(O(B)\). If rank is \(r\), the span has \(2^{r}\) distinct values. For representation counts from \(n\) input vectors, every reachable value has \(2^{n-r}\) representations. To obtain the zero-indexed \(k\)-th smallest distinct XOR, reduce to a basis in which every pivot bit occurs in only its own vector, order those vectors by increasing pivot bit, and XOR the vectors selected by the bits of \(k\). A merely triangular or arbitrarily ordered basis does not give numeric order.
Graph recognition: assign each vertex an XOR distance from a DFS root. Every non-tree edge yields a cycle XOR dist[u] ^ w ^ dist[v]. If \(s,t\) lie in the same undirected connected component, all XORs of walks from \(s\) to \(t\) are dist[s]^dist[t] plus the span of that component’s cycle XORs.



For a weighted undirected graph, form the Laplacian
\[L_{ii}=\sum_{j\ne i}w_{ij},\qquad L_{ij}=-w_{ij}\quad(i\ne j).\]
The diagonal is the total edge weight leaving a vertex; an off-diagonal entry is the negative edge weight connecting its two vertices (with parallel-edge weights added first). Delete any one row and the corresponding column. The determinant of the resulting \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) cofactor equals the total weight of spanning trees, where a tree’s weight is the product of its edge weights.
Why it works: orient edges arbitrarily and let \(B\) be the incidence matrix. Then \(L=BWB^{T}\). Cauchy–Binet expands a cofactor determinant over sets of edges. A set with a cycle or a disconnected vertex has zero determinant; exactly a spanning tree has incidence determinant \(\pm1\), whose square is one. Directed arborescences require a directional convention. With \(L_{ii}=\sum_{i\to j,\ j\ne i}w_{ij}\) and, for \(i\ne j\), \(L_{ij}=-\sum_{\text{edges }i\to j}w_{ij}\), the root cofactor counts trees whose edges point toward the root. To count trees pointing away from the root, use the indegree convention \(L_{ii}=\sum_{j\to i,\ j\ne i}w_{ji}\), \(L_{ij}=-\sum_{\text{edges }j\to i}w_{ji}\). On the one-edge graph \(r\to v\), deleting the row and column of \(r\) gives determinant \(1\) only under the indegree convention, as required for the unique tree pointing away from \(r\). This two-vertex test catches a transposed convention.
Complexity is \(O(n^{3})\) with dense elimination. Parallel edge weights add. Self-loops do not contribute. Under a modulus, the determinant counts modulo that modulus.
For a triangle with unit edge weights, deleting one row and column leaves \(\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\), whose determinant is \(3\). These are exactly the three spanning trees obtained by deleting one edge.



If \(s_n=c_1s_{n-1}+\cdots+c_ks_{n-k}\), then the polynomial \(x^{k}-c_1x^{k-1}-\cdots-c_k\) annihilates the sequence: replace every \(x^k\) by the prescribed combination of lower powers. Reduce \(x^{N}\) modulo this polynomial; the remainder coefficients tell exactly how to combine \(s_0,\ldots,s_{k-1}\) to obtain \(s_N\). Binary exponentiation with polynomial reduction costs \(O(k^{2}\log N)\) (Kitamasa); NTT-based methods or Bostan–Mori improve large \(k\).
For Fibonacci, the characteristic polynomial is \(x^2-x-1\). Since \(x^5\equiv5x+3\pmod{x^2-x-1}\), every Fibonacci-type sequence obeys \(s_5=3s_0+5s_1\). This is what “the remainder coefficients tell how to combine initial terms” means concretely.
If the true shortest recurrence has order \(L\), Berlekamp–Massey recovers it from \(2L\) exact terms over a field. Preconditions: exact field arithmetic and enough terms; a short prefix can admit a spurious recurrence.
Cayley–Hamilton says a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. Thus every scalar sequence \(u^T A^n v\) has order at most the matrix dimension. This bridges matrix exponentiation, recurrences, and generating functions.



For dense matrices, Hessenberg reduction followed by the determinant recurrence computes the characteristic polynomial in \(O(n^{3})\). Determinant interpolation at \(n+1\) points is simpler but \(O(n^{4})\) with naive determinants.
For a huge sparse matrix, dense elimination wastes work on zeroes. Wiedemann chooses random vectors \(u,v\), generates \(a_i=u^T A^i v\), and applies Berlekamp–Massey. With enough terms, this recovers the scalar sequence’s minimal polynomial exactly; random projection makes it equal to the matrix’s minimal polynomial with high probability, with a bound that depends on the field and invariant factors. Applications include sparse linear systems and determinants after random diagonal preconditioning.
Assumptions and failure modes:

It is randomized; a projection can miss invariant factors. Repeat independently.
Field size should be comfortably large. Extension fields or several primes reduce failure probability.
One sparse matrix-vector multiply must be fast; otherwise dense elimination is safer.
Recovering a determinant requires more than the scalar recurrence: use a proven preconditioning recipe and account for the preconditioner’s determinant.





Division modulo a composite number silently invalidates Gaussian elimination.
Partial pivoting is essential over floating point, but “largest pivot” has no meaning in a finite field.
A determinant changes sign on every row swap.
A graph XOR basis uses cycle values, not raw edge weights.
Kirchhoff counts multigraph edges separately; collapsing them without adding weights changes the answer.
Berlekamp–Massey coefficient sign conventions differ among templates. Verify on Fibonacci before a contest.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
Over a field, row operations preserve the solution set because they merely replace one equation by an equivalent linear combination of equations. Maintain a pivot row; for each column choose a nonzero entry, swap it to that row, normalize, and eliminate. A pivot in the coefficient matrix records one independent equation, so \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) is the number of such pivots. For a system with \(r\) equations and \(c\) unknowns, a zero row with a nonzero augmented entry means inconsistency; otherwise the augmented matrix has the same rank as \(A\) and there are \(c-\operatorname{rank}(A)\) free variables. Over \(\mathbb F_q\), that means exactly \(q^{\,c-\operatorname{rank}(A)}\) solutions; over an infinite field it describes a solution affine space of that dimension.
For example, over \(\mathbb F_5\), \(x+y=1\), \(2x+3y=0\) becomes \(y=3,x=3\) after subtracting twice the first row. The integer solution is irrelevant: the field is part of the question. Dense elimination costs \(O(rc\min(r,c))\). For determinant, do not normalize: each row swap negates the answer, multiply by the pivot, then eliminate below using the current entry divided by the pivot. Composite moduli are not fields: a nonzero pivot may be noninvertible. Use prime-factor methods, fraction-free elimination, or exact integer algorithms instead.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
A set of machine words is a vector set whose coordinates are bits, with XOR as vector addition. Keep at most one pivot per highest bit. Inserting a word means XORing away known highest bits; if nothing remains it was already a linear combination of earlier words, otherwise it adds one independent direction.
Insertion costs \(O(B)\). If rank is \(r\), the span has \(2^{r}\) distinct values. For representation counts from \(n\) input vectors, every reachable value has \(2^{n-r}\) representations. To obtain the zero-indexed \(k\)-th smallest distinct XOR, reduce to a basis in which every pivot bit occurs in only its own vector, order those vectors by increasing pivot bit, and XOR the vectors selected by the bits of \(k\). A merely triangular or arbitrarily ordered basis does not give numeric order.
Graph recognition: assign each vertex an XOR distance from a DFS root. Every non-tree edge yields a cycle XOR dist[u] ^ w ^ dist[v]. If \(s,t\) lie in the same undirected connected component, all XORs of walks from \(s\) to \(t\) are dist[s]^dist[t] plus the span of that component’s cycle XORs.

title: 10 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields
text:
For a weighted undirected graph, form the Laplacian
\[L_{ii}=\sum_{j\ne i}w_{ij},\qquad L_{ij}=-w_{ij}\quad(i\ne j).\]
The diagonal is the total edge weight leaving a vertex; an off-diagonal entry is the negative edge weight connecting its two vertices (with parallel-edge weights added first). Delete any one row and the corresponding column. The determinant of the resulting \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) cofactor equals the total weight of spanning trees, where a tree’s weight is the product of its edge weights.
Why it works: orient edges arbitrarily and let \(B\) be the incidence matrix. Then \(L=BWB^{T}\). Cauchy–Binet expands a cofactor determinant over sets of edges. A set with a cycle or a disconnected vertex has zero determinant; exactly a spanning tree has incidence determinant \(\pm1\), whose square is one. Directed arborescences require a directional convention. With \(L_{ii}=\sum_{i\to j,\ j\ne i}w_{ij}\) and, for \(i\ne j\), \(L_{ij}=-\sum_{\text{edges }i\to j}w_{ij}\), the root cofactor counts trees whose edges point toward the root. To count trees pointing away from the root, use the indegree convention \(L_{ii}=\sum_{j\to i,\ j\ne i}w_{ji}\), \(L_{ij}=-\sum_{\text{edges }j\to i}w_{ji}\). On the one-edge graph \(r\to v\), deleting the row and column of \(r\) gives determinant \(1\) only under the indegree convention, as required for the unique tree pointing away from \(r\). This two-vertex test catches a transposed convention.
Complexity is \(O(n^{3})\) with dense elimination. Parallel edge weights add. Self-loops do not contribute. Under a modulus, the determinant counts modulo that modulus.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
Combinatorics is not primarily a collection of formulas. It is the job of describing exactly what one valid object is, then counting those objects without losing or duplicating any of them. This chapter starts from that description. It assumes that factorials and binomial coefficients are already in your library, but it does not assume that you have previously seen the counting models below.
Before doing algebra, write four answers on paper:

What is one object I am counting?
Are its atoms labelled (distinguishable)?
Does the order of components matter?
Which restrictions are hard, and is their intersection easier to count?

Those answers prevent most wrong applications of a correct formula.










Wording in a statement
First model to try
The question to ask next




every required property is present
inclusion–exclusion (IE) over missing properties
can I count an intersection of chosen missing properties?


exactly/at least \(k\) properties
binomial inversion or weighted IE
how many selected conditions does each object satisfy?


partition labelled objects into unlabeled nonempty groups
Stirling numbers of the second kind
are the groups really unordered?


cycles of a permutation
unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind
where can the new label be inserted?


recursively nested/balanced/plane-tree object
Catalan decomposition
does the first return/root split it independently?


sum over subsets whose term depends only on its size
binomial transform
can factorial scaling turn it into convolution?


forbidden row–column assignments
rook polynomial
are selected forbidden assignments compatible?



For example, “put \(n\) students into \(k\) nonempty teams” has labelled students but unlabelled teams. “Assign every student one of \(k\) named rooms” has labelled rooms. The two answers differ by a factor of \(k!\); it is not a minor implementation detail.



Suppose \(U\) is the set of all candidate objects and \(E_i\) is the set of objects violating requirement \(i\). We want objects in none of the bad sets:
\[|U\setminus(E_1\cup\cdots\cup E_m)|.\]
The easy count \(|U|\) includes bad objects. Subtracting every \(|E_i|\) removes an object that violates two requirements twice, so it is now missing once too many. Add pair intersections back; then three-way intersections are too large again; and so on. The resulting formula is
\[
|U\setminus\textstyle\bigcup_i E_i|
=\sum_{S\subseteq[m]}(-1)^{|S|}\left|\bigcap_{i\in S}E_i\right|. \tag{IE}
\]
The empty intersection is \(U\). Formula (IE) is safest when understood per object: if a particular object violates exactly \(t\) requirements, it occurs in \(\binom{t}{j}\) intersections of size \(j\), so its total coefficient is
\[\sum_{j=0}^{t}(-1)^j\binom tj=(1-1)^t.\]
It is \(1\) for a valid object (\(t=0\)) and \(0\) otherwise. This tells us exactly what IE is calculating: it filters all candidates down to candidates with no bad property.


How many functions from \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) to \([k]\) use every one of the \(k\) targets? There are \(k^n\) unrestricted functions. Let \(E_j\) mean “target \(j\) is unused.” If we insist that a chosen set \(S\) of \(i\) targets is unused, each input has only \(k-i\) possible images, so the intersection has \((k-i)^n\) functions. There are \(\binom ki\) choices of \(S\). Thus
\[\#\text{surjections}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^i\binom ki(k-i)^n. \tag{1}\]
Notice the separate meaning of every factor: choose which forbidden targets are absent, then count functions that avoid all of them. IE is useful here because intersections are simpler than “uses every target” directly.



Sometimes the target is not “none of the bad events.” Let \(a_j\) be the number of objects satisfying exactly \(j\) of \(m\) conditions. Let \(b_k\) count pairs
\[\bigl(\text{object},\ \text{a chosen set of $k$ conditions it satisfies}\bigr).\]
An object satisfying exactly \(j\) conditions contributes \(\binom jk\) such pairs, so double counting gives
\[b_k=\sum_{j\ge k}\binom jk a_j. \tag{2}\]
Binomial inversion undoes that “choose \(k\) among \(j\)” operation:
\[a_r=\sum_{k=r}^{m}(-1)^{k-r}\binom kr b_k. \tag{3}\]
Use (2) to derive the quantity you can count, and (3) only after you know what \(b_k\) means. This prevents the common mistake of alternating signs without a defined universe.






The second-kind Stirling number \(\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}\) is the number of ways to split \(n\) labelled elements into \(k\) nonempty unlabelled blocks. Consider where label \(n\) goes. Either it joins one of the existing \(k\) blocks of a partition of \([n-1]\), or it forms its own block beside a partition into \(k-1\) blocks. Therefore
\[
\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}
=k\left\{ {n-1\atop k}\right\}
+\left\{ {n-1\atop k-1}\right\}. \tag{4}
\]
For instance, \(\left\{ {3\atop2}\right\}=3\): the singleton can be \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\). If the \(k\) blocks are then assigned to \(k\) named targets, there are \(k!\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}\) functions using every target. Comparing this with (1) explains, rather than merely states,
\[\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}={1\over k!}\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^{k-i}\binom ki i^n.\]
This is first an identity of integers. If it is evaluated by dividing in a coefficient ring, \(k!\) must be a unit; over \(\mathbb F_p\) the usual factorial-inverse route therefore requires \(k<p\).
The unsigned first-kind number \(\left[ {n\atop k}\right]\) counts permutations of \([n]\) having \(k\) cycles. To add label \(n\), either make it a one-element cycle, or insert it immediately after any of the \(n-1\) existing labels in a cycle. This gives
\[
\left[ {n\atop k}\right]
=(n-1)\left[ {n-1\atop k}\right]
+\left[ {n-1\atop k-1}\right]. \tag{5}
\]



Catalan numbers count many objects because those objects have the same decomposition. A balanced-parenthesis string is either empty, or has the form
( a balanced string ) another balanced string. The first matching ) creates this split uniquely. If \(C_n\) counts strings with \(n\) pairs, choosing \(i\) pairs inside the first pair leaves \(n-1-i\) pairs after it, so
\[C_0=1,\qquad C_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}C_iC_{n-1-i}. \tag{6}\]
The product appears because the two pieces can be chosen independently. With \(C(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}C_nx^n\), (6) becomes \(C(x)=1+xC(x)^2\), from which
\[C_n={1\over n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.\]
One direct derivation views a parenthesis string as a path with an up-step for ( and a down-step for ). There are \(\binom{2n}{n}\) paths ending at height zero. Reflect the prefix through the first step below zero; this bijects the bad paths with paths having \(n+1\) up-steps and \(n-1\) down-steps, of which there are \(\binom{2n}{n+1}=\binom{2n}{n-1}\). Therefore
\[
C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}
=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
This quotient is an integer combinatorially; when evaluating it in a field, also require \(n+1\) to be invertible (or compute it as an integer before reducing). Do not apply the formula merely because parentheses or trees appear: verify the unique, independent split first.



An integer partition ignores the order of parts. For a part size \(j\), we may use it zero, one, two, … times, contributing the size-marking series
\[1+x^j+x^{2j}+\cdots={1\over1-x^j}.\]
Choices for different sizes are independent, so multiply them:
\[P(x)=\prod_{j\ge1}{1\over1-x^j}. \tag{7}\]
This infinite product is formal: to determine \([x^n]P\), factors with \(j>n\) can be replaced by \(1\), so every requested coefficient depends on only finitely many choices.
For \(n=4\), the coefficient of \(x^4\) represents \(4\), \(3+1\), \(2+2\), \(2+1+1\), and \(1+1+1+1\). If each size can be used once, replace the relevant factor by \(1+x^j\); if only some sizes are allowed, omit the others. The product comes from a modelling decision, not from a pattern to memorise.




The binomial transform
\[b_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a_k\]
looks quadratic for all \(n\). Expand the binomial coefficient:
\[
b_n=n!\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{a_k}{k!}\frac1{(n-k)!}. \tag{8}
\]
The right side is the coefficient of \(x^n\) in the product of the two ordinary polynomials whose coefficients are \(a_k/k!\) and \(1/k!\). Thus one convolution, followed by multiplying coefficient \(n\) by \(n!\), computes all \(b_n\).
This is a change of representation: labelled choices produce \(\binom nk\); dividing by factorials changes “choose labels” into ordinary convolution. It requires the factorials through the desired degree to be invertible, normally a prime modulus larger than that degree. See Chapter 06 for the convolution contract.



This section answers a very specific question clearly.
There are \(n\) people and \(n\) jobs. A permutation \(\pi\) is a complete assignment: person \(i\) receives job \(\pi(i)\), with every job used once. Draw an \(n\times n\) board. Row \(i\), column \(j\) is a forbidden cell when person \(i\) may not receive job \(j\). We want the number of permutations that avoid every forbidden cell.
For each forbidden cell \((i,j)\), define the bad event
\[E_{i,j}=\{\pi:\pi(i)=j\}.\]
IE says to sum over sets \(S\) of forbidden assignments that are all forced to happen. But an intersection is impossible if \(S\) asks one person to take two jobs, or two people to take one job. The possible sets are exactly placements of nonattacking rooks on forbidden cells: no two share a row or a column.
Let \(r_k\) be the number of ways to place \(k\) such rooks. Fix one placement. It forces \(k\) person–job pairs, and the remaining \(n-k\) people can be matched to the remaining \(n-k\) jobs in exactly \((n-k)!\) ways. Every placement with \(k\) rooks therefore contributes the same intersection size. Grouping IE terms by \(k\) gives
\[
\boxed{\#\text{valid assignments}
=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k r_k(n-k)!}. \tag{9}
\]
So IE in (9) is calculating the number of complete assignments that use no forbidden cell. \(r_k\) is not the number of assignments; it counts the compatible ways to force \(k\) forbidden assignments while performing IE.


Suppose \(n=3\) and the forbidden cells are \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\). The rook counts are \(r_0=1\), \(r_1=2\), \(r_2=1\): place no rook; choose either cell; or choose both cells, which do not share a row or column. Formula (9) gives
\[3!-2\cdot2!+1\cdot1!=6-4+1=3.\]
Indeed the valid permutations are \((2,1,3)\), \((2,3,1)\), and \((3,1,2)\).
Package the rook counts as a polynomial
\[R_B(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}r_kz^k,\]
where \(B\) is the forbidden board. If the forbidden cells split into two parts using disjoint sets of rows and columns, a nonattacking placement is an independent placement in each part. Consequently
\[R_{B_1\cup B_2}(z)=R_{B_1}(z)R_{B_2}(z).\]
For example, \(t\) isolated forbidden cells in distinct rows and columns have \(R_B(z)=(1+z)^t\). This product rule is valuable only after checking that the components share neither a person nor a job; disconnected-looking cells that share a row are not independent.




When a formula is unfamiliar, reconstruct it with this sequence:

Name the candidates and the desired subset.
State what one term or one coefficient counts.
Explain why choices multiply or why cases add.
Test the result on \(n=0,1,2\) or a hand-enumerable board.
Only then choose a DP, convolution, or generating-function implementation.

Common errors are conceptual rather than syntactic:

confusing \(k!\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}\) named groups with \(\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}\) unnamed groups;
dividing by \(k!\) although it is zero modulo the chosen characteristic;
using IE when intersections are harder than the original condition;
using a rook product although board pieces share a row or column;
counting rotations/reflections as distinct when the problem regards them as identical (continue to Chapter 05).

Continue to group actions for symmetry, or to polynomials for fast transforms.

+\left\{ {n-1\atop k-1}\right\}. \tag{4}
\]
For instance, \(\left\{ {3\atop2}\right\}=3\): the singleton can be \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\). If the \(k\) blocks are then assigned to \(k\) named targets, there are \(k!\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}\) functions using every target. Comparing this with (1) explains, rather than merely states,
\[\left\{ {n\atop k}\right\}={1\over k!}\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^{k-i}\binom ki i^n.\]
This is first an identity of integers. If it is evaluated by dividing in a coefficient ring, \(k!\) must be a unit; over \(\mathbb F_p\) the usual factorial-inverse route therefore requires \(k<p\).
The unsigned first-kind number \(\left[ {n\atop k}\right]\) counts permutations of \([n]\) having \(k\) cycles. To add label \(n\), either make it a one-element cycle, or insert it immediately after any of the \(n-1\) existing labels in a cycle. This gives
\[
\left[ {n\atop k}\right]
=(n-1)\left[ {n-1\atop k}\right]
+\left[ {n-1\atop k-1}\right]. \tag{5}
\]



Catalan numbers count many objects because those objects have the same decomposition. A balanced-parenthesis string is either empty, or has the form
( a balanced string ) another balanced string. The first matching ) creates this split uniquely. If \(C_n\) counts strings with \(n\) pairs, choosing \(i\) pairs inside the first pair leaves \(n-1-i\) pairs after it, so
\[C_0=1,\qquad C_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}C_iC_{n-1-i}. \tag{6}\]
The product appears because the two pieces can be chosen independently. With \(C(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}C_nx^n\), (6) becomes \(C(x)=1+xC(x)^2\), from which
\[C_n={1\over n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.\]
One direct derivation views a parenthesis string as a path with an up-step for ( and a down-step for ). There are \(\binom{2n}{n}\) paths ending at height zero. Reflect the prefix through the first step below zero; this bijects the bad paths with paths having \(n+1\) up-steps and \(n-1\) down-steps, of which there are \(\binom{2n}{n+1}=\binom{2n}{n-1}\). Therefore
\[
C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}
=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
This quotient is an integer combinatorially; when evaluating it in a field, also require \(n+1\) to be invertible (or compute it as an integer before reducing). Do not apply the formula merely because parentheses or trees appear: verify the unique, independent split first.



An integer partition ignores the order of parts. For a part size \(j\), we may use it zero, one, two, … times, contributing the size-marking series
\[1+x^j+x^{2j}+\cdots={1\over1-x^j}.\]
Choices for different sizes are independent, so multiply them:
\[P(x)=\prod_{j\ge1}{1\over1-x^j}. \tag{7}\]
This infinite product is formal: to determine \([x^n]P\), factors with \(j>n\) can be replaced by \(1\), so every requested coefficient depends on only finitely many choices.
For \(n=4\), the coefficient of \(x^4\) represents \(4\), \(3+1\), \(2+2\), \(2+1+1\), and \(1+1+1+1\). If each size can be used once, replace the relevant factor by \(1+x^j\); if only some sizes are allowed, omit the others. The product comes from a modelling decision, not from a pattern to memorise.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
The binomial transform
\[b_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a_k\]
looks quadratic for all \(n\). Expand the binomial coefficient:
\[
b_n=n!\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{a_k}{k!}\frac1{(n-k)!}. \tag{8}
\]
The right side is the coefficient of \(x^n\) in the product of the two ordinary polynomials whose coefficients are \(a_k/k!\) and \(1/k!\). Thus one convolution, followed by multiplying coefficient \(n\) by \(n!\), computes all \(b_n\).
This is a change of representation: labelled choices produce \(\binom nk\); dividing by factorials changes “choose labels” into ordinary convolution. It requires the factorials through the desired degree to be invertible, normally a prime modulus larger than that degree. See Chapter 06 for the convolution contract.

title: 04 — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
This section answers a very specific question clearly.
There are \(n\) people and \(n\) jobs. A permutation \(\pi\) is a complete assignment: person \(i\) receives job \(\pi(i)\), with every job used once. Draw an \(n\times n\) board. Row \(i\), column \(j\) is a forbidden cell when person \(i\) may not receive job \(j\). We want the number of permutations that avoid every forbidden cell.
For each forbidden cell \((i,j)\), define the bad event
\[E_{i,j}=\{\pi:\pi(i)=j\}.\]
IE says to sum over sets \(S\) of forbidden assignments that are all forced to happen. But an intersection is impossible if \(S\) asks one person to take two jobs, or two people to take one job. The possible sets are exactly placements of nonattacking rooks on forbidden cells: no two share a row or a column.
Let \(r_k\) be the number of ways to place \(k\) such rooks. Fix one placement. It forces \(k\) person–job pairs, and the remaining \(n-k\) people can be matched to the remaining \(n-k\) jobs in exactly \((n-k)!\) ways. Every placement with \(k\) rooks therefore contributes the same intersection size. Grouping IE terms by \(k\) gives
\[
\boxed{\#\text{valid assignments}
=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k r_k(n-k)!}. \tag{9}
\]
So IE in (9) is calculating the number of complete assignments that use no forbidden cell. \(r_k\) is not the number of assignments; it counts the compatible ways to force \(k\) forbidden assignments while performing IE.


Suppose \(n=3\) and the forbidden cells are \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\). The rook counts are \(r_0=1\), \(r_1=2\), \(r_2=1\): place no rook; choose either cell; or choose both cells, which do not share a row or column. Formula (9) gives
\[3!-2\cdot2!+1\cdot1!=6-4+1=3.\]
Indeed the valid permutations are \((2,1,3)\), \((2,3,1)\), and \((3,1,2)\).
Package the rook counts as a polynomial
\[R_B(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}r_kz^k,\]
where \(B\) is the forbidden board. If the forbidden cells split into two parts using disjoint sets of rows and columns, a nonattacking placement is an independent placement in each part. Consequently
\[R_{B_1\cup B_2}(z)=R_{B_1}(z)R_{B_2}(z).\]
For example, \(t\) isolated forbidden cells in distinct rows and columns have \(R_B(z)=(1+z)^t\). This product rule is valuable only after checking that the components share neither a person nor a job; disconnected-looking cells that share a row are not independent.

title: 19 — Frontier Capstones
text:
This is a synthesis chapter, not a source of new machinery. Read Chapters 14–18 first, then attempt a problem before reopening the relevant chapter. A capstone is successful when you can explain the reduction in ordinary words: what an algebraic coefficient represents, why the operation preserves that meaning, and why every division or randomized step is legal.
Allow 3–5 team-hours per problem. Before coding, write a one-page proposal: the algebraic object, its coefficient domain, the invariant or theorem that connects it to the statement, target complexity, and any randomized error bound. This turns “try a transform” into a testable model.



make 1 — ABC278 Ex. Model rank growth of vectors over \(\mathbb F_2\) and recognize a Gaussian binomial count.


After an honest attempt

Review Gaussian binomials: the key object is a subspace, not a collection of independent coordinates.

Long Binary String — CF1698G. Translate repeated shifts into multiplication in \(\mathbb F_2[x]\) and use factor information.


After an honest attempt

Review finite-field factorization. State exactly which quotient ring represents the allowed operations.

Lights Out on Connected Graph — ARC105 F. Count all labelled objects first, then extract the connected contribution.


After an honest attempt

Review set-series exp/log. Identify the unique connected-component partition before applying a logarithm.

Degree Harmony — ABC412 G. Turn a constrained matching question into the lowest nonzero term of a determinant polynomial.


After an honest attempt

Review Tutte matrices and write the Schwartz–Zippel degree bound for the exact polynomial you evaluate.

Chinese Elephant Chess — QOJ 60. Compress a labelled component model to a differential equation and a P-recurrence.


After an honest attempt

Review the series/sequence bridge. A recurrence is useful only after its initial values and singular indices are specified.

Graphs — QOJ 11139. Replace a formidable multiple sum with a certified polynomial-coefficient recurrence.


After an honest attempt

Review guessing and certification. Empirical agreement supplies a conjecture, not the final proof.





For each problem, record the recognition clue, algebraic model, preconditions, target complexity, randomized error bound if any, and the smallest brute-force oracle that could have caught the first bug. Also write one sentence naming the first tempting but wrong tool—for example, ordinary subset convolution when labels may overlap, or factorial division when a denominator is a non-unit.
